lessons.title: Ionic bonding
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is salt a hard crystal that melts only at 801 °C?
objectives: Predict ion charges from the Periodic Table and write ionic formulae
Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for ionic compounds
Explain the properties of ionic compounds
successCriteria: All: describe electron transfer
Most: write formulae and draw diagrams
Some: explain melting points and conductivity using charge and the lattice
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: electrostatics; Geography: salt deposits
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: order in matter; the discovery that simple rules explain many substances

keywords.def: charged particle formed by loss or gain of electrons
strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
regular repeating arrangement of ions
ionic compound that conducts when molten or dissolved

starter: Bismillah. Write the electronic configuration of sodium (atomic number 11) and chlorine (17).
What is the charge on a proton and an electron?
Define a compound.

teach.heading: Electron transfer
bullets: Metal atoms lose electrons to become positive ions
Non-metal atoms gain electrons to become negative ions
Full outer shell: noble-gas configuration
teach.note: Na (2,8,1) → Na⁺ (2,8) by losing one electron; Cl (2,8,7) → Cl⁻ (2,8,8) by gaining one. Magnesium oxide: Mg (2,8,2) gives two electrons to O (2,6). Dot-and-cross diagrams show outer shells only, with brackets and charges. Practise drawing on the board.

head: Group
Typical ion
Examples
rows: Zn²⁺, Ag⁺, NH₄⁺, OH⁻, NO₃⁻, CO₃²⁻, SO₄²⁻

teach.heading: Writing formulae
bullets: Balance the total positive and negative charge
Brackets around polyatomic ions when more than one
The compound has no overall charge
teach.note: Show the criss-cross trick but insist on checking charges: Al³⁺ and O²⁻ need 2 Al (+6) and 3 O (−6), so Al₂O₃. Ca²⁺ and NO₃⁻ gives Ca(NO₃)₂. Cu²⁺ with SO₄²⁻ gives CuSO₄.

model.problem: Write the formula of aluminium oxide and of ammonium sulfate.
steps: Al³⁺ and O²⁻: lowest common multiple of charge is 6
NH₄⁺ and SO₄²⁻: need 2 NH₄⁺ for each SO₄²⁻

teach.heading: Properties and why
bullets: High melting point: strong attractions in the giant lattice
Do not conduct when solid; ions fixed in place
Conduct when molten or dissolved: ions free to move
teach.note: Data: sodium chloride melts at 801 °C and magnesium oxide at about 2850 °C. MgO ions have charges of 2+ and 2−, so stronger attractions need more energy to separate. Many ionic compounds dissolve in water.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils say free electrons carry the current in molten NaCl. Ions carry charge in the liquid.

check.q: Why does molten sodium chloride conduct electricity?
check.why: In the molten state the ions are free to move and carry charge. In the solid the ions are fixed in the lattice.

practice: Describe what happens to the electrons when magnesium reacts with oxygen.
Write the formulae for calcium chloride and lithium oxide.
Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct?
independent: Core: Draw dot-and-cross diagrams (outer shells) for NaCl and MgO.
Extend: Explain why magnesium oxide has a much higher melting point than sodium chloride. [3 marks]
Stretch: Explain why ionic compounds are brittle when hit with a hammer. [2 marks]
exit: Give the formula of aluminium sulfate. [1 mark]
Return to the big question using the word lattice.
lessons.homework: Draw and label a giant ionic lattice and write six formulae of ionic compounds.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: charge-balance cards. Stretch: how does lattice enthalpy relate to melting point?

lessons.title: Covalent bonding and simple molecules
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is methane a gas but sodium chloride a solid when both are 'compounds'?
objectives: Describe a covalent bond as a shared pair of electrons
Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for simple molecules
Explain the properties of simple molecular substances
successCriteria: All: explain a covalent bond
Most: draw dot-and-cross diagrams for common molecules
Some: explain boiling point trends and conductivity
lessons.crossCurricular: Biology: molecules of life; Physics: forces
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at the small scale of creation

keywords.def: shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms
group of atoms joined by covalent bonds
weak force between molecules
substance made of small molecules with weak forces between them

starter: Bismillah. Write the electronic configuration of carbon and oxygen.
Define an ionic bond.
State the formula of ammonia.

teach.heading: Sharing electrons
bullets: Non-metal atoms share pairs to fill outer shells
Each shared pair is one covalent bond
Double bond: two shared pairs (O₂, CO₂)
teach.note: Examples to draw: H₂, Cl₂, HCl, H₂O, NH₃, CH₄, O₂, N₂ (triple bond), CO₂. Count outer electrons first, then share. Unshared outer pairs are lone pairs.

teach.heading: Model: draw ammonia
bullets: Count outer electrons
Share to complete the shells
Show lone pairs
teach.note: Talk through drawing three hydrogen electrons (crosses) shared with N (dots): N has five outer electrons, needs three more for eight; each H needs one to fill its shell of two.

model.problem: Draw (describe) a dot-and-cross diagram for ammonia, NH₃.
steps: N has 5 outer electrons, H has 1 each
N shares one pair with each of three H atoms
Each H has 2 electrons, N has 3 shared pairs + 1 lone pair = 8
Total: 3 covalent bonds and one lone pair on N
model.answer: N with three shared pairs to H atoms and one lone pair

teach.heading: Properties of simple molecules
bullets: Low melting and boiling points
Weak intermolecular forces broken, not covalent bonds
No charged particles, so no conduction
teach.note: Trend: bigger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so higher boiling points. Data: CH₄ −162 °C, Cl₂ −34 °C, Br₂ 59 °C.

misconception.wrong: When ice melts or ethanol boils, covalent bonds inside the molecules break.
misconception.right: Only the weak forces between molecules are overcome; the covalent bonds inside each molecule stay intact.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils recall 'strong bonds' and choose ionic or lattice explanations. Remember that it is the intermolecular forces that matter.

check.q: Which statement best explains the low boiling point of methane?
check.why: Methane is a small molecule held by weak forces between molecules, so little energy is needed to separate them.

practice: Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for HCl and Cl₂.
How many shared pairs are in a nitrogen molecule?
Why do covalent substances like methane not conduct?
independent: Core: Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for water and methane.
Extend: Draw CO₂ and explain why the carbon–oxygen bonds are double bonds. [3 marks]
Stretch: Explain why the boiling points rise from chlorine to bromine to iodine. [3 marks]
exit: Describe what a covalent bond is. [2 marks]
Return to the big question in two sentences.
lessons.homework: Make a poster comparing ionic and covalent bonding with a worked example of each.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-drawn outlines to add electrons. Stretch: how are coordinate (dative) bonds different?

lessons.title: Giant covalent structures and metallic bonding
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is diamond hard but pencil lead slippery when both are carbon?
objectives: Describe the structures of diamond, graphite, silicon dioxide and C60
Explain properties from bonding and structure
Describe metallic bonding and explain properties of metals
successCriteria: All: name the structures and a use
Most: link structure to properties
Some: explain why graphite conducts and compare allotropes
lessons.crossCurricular: Engineering: materials; Art: pencils and jewellery
lessons.smsc: Moral: responsible mining and use of materials

keywords.def: different structural forms of the same element
millions of atoms joined by covalent bonds in a lattice
electron free to move through a structure
attraction between metal ions and delocalised electrons

starter: Bismillah. State two properties of simple molecular substances.
Name the group that carbon is in.
What is a covalent bond?

teach.heading: Carbon allotropes
bullets: Diamond: each C bonded to four others
Graphite: each C bonded to three, in layers
C60 fullerene: a hollow ball of 60 carbon atoms
teach.note: Diamond: very hard, very high melting point, no conduction (no free electrons). Graphite: soft and slippery as layers slide (weak forces between layers), conducts because the fourth electron per atom is delocalised. C60 is a simple molecular substance, so it has weak forces between molecules and is soft.

teach.heading: Silicon dioxide
bullets: Giant lattice of Si and O
Each Si bonded to four O
Very high melting point, hard, does not conduct
teach.note: Sand and quartz. Melting point about 1700 °C because many strong covalent bonds must be broken.

model.problem: Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not. [3 marks]
steps: In graphite each carbon uses three of its four outer electrons for bonds
The fourth electron is delocalised and free to move
Delocalised electrons carry charge through the layers
In diamond all four electrons are used in bonds, so none are free
model.answer: Graphite has delocalised electrons; diamond does not.

teach.heading: Metallic bonding
bullets: Positive ions in a regular lattice
Sea of delocalised electrons
Strong attraction between ions and electrons
teach.note: Properties: conduct electricity and heat because electrons move; malleable and ductile as layers of ions slide over each other while the electrons hold them together; high melting points. Alloys are harder because different-sized atoms disrupt the layers.

right.title: Ionic compounds
points: Conduct only when molten or dissolved

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils think C60 is giant covalent because it is made of carbon only.

check.q: Which substance is made of small molecules with weak forces between them?
check.why: C60 is a simple molecular substance. The other three are giant covalent.

practice: List the number of bonds per carbon atom in diamond and in graphite.
Explain why metals can be hammered into shape.
State one use of graphite and one of diamond.
independent: Core: Make a table comparing diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide.
Extend: Explain why graphite is used as a lubricant. [2 marks]
Stretch: Compare the bonding and properties of copper and sodium chloride. [4 marks]
exit: Name the particles that move in a metal when it conducts. [1 mark]
Return to the big question: explain the difference between diamond and graphite.
lessons.homework: Draw labelled diagrams of diamond, graphite and a metallic lattice.

lessons.title: Electrolysis of molten and aqueous electrolytes
lessons.bigQuestion: How does electricity pull a metal out of a liquid?
objectives: Describe electrolysis and name the electrodes
Predict the products of molten and aqueous electrolytes
Write half-equations and identify oxidation and reduction
successCriteria: All: describe electrolysis and name the electrodes
Most: predict products and test the gases
Some: write half-equations and interpret oxidation and reduction
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: electric current; Industry: extraction and plating
lessons.smsc: Moral: using energy responsibly in industry

keywords.def: breaking down an ionic compound using electricity
positive electrode
negative electrode
equation showing electron transfer at one electrode

starter: Bismillah. Why do molten ionic compounds conduct?
Write the formula of lead(II) bromide.
What is an ion?

teach.heading: Electrolysis set-up
bullets: Electrolyte is molten or dissolved ionic compound
Positive ions go to the cathode (negative)
Negative ions go to the anode (positive)
teach.note: Use an inert electrode (graphite or platinum). Electrons flow in the wires; ions carry charge through the electrolyte. Molten lead(II) bromide: lead at the cathode, bromine at the anode (do this as a teacher demonstration in a fume cupboard only).

teach.heading: Half-equations
bullets: Cathode: reduction (gain of electrons)
Anode: oxidation (loss of electrons)
OIL RIG
teach.note: At the cathode: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb; 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂; Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. At the anode: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻; 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻; 4OH⁻ → 2H₂O + O₂ + 4e⁻. Gas tests: H₂ squeaky pop; O₂ relights glowing splint; Cl₂ bleaches damp litmus.

model.problem: Predict the products of electrolysing aqueous sodium chloride with inert electrodes. Explain. [4 marks]
steps: Ions present: Na⁺, Cl⁻, H⁺, OH⁻
Cathode: hydrogen forms because sodium is more reactive than hydrogen
Anode: chloride is discharged to give chlorine (concentrated solution)
Sodium and hydroxide ions remain, forming sodium hydroxide solution
model.answer: Hydrogen at the cathode, chlorine at the anode, sodium hydroxide in solution

teach.heading: Rules for aqueous solutions
bullets: Cathode: metal if less reactive than hydrogen, else hydrogen
Anode: halogen from halide ions, else oxygen
Practical: test gases and observe changes
teach.note: Core practical: electrolyse copper(II) sulfate solution with graphite electrodes: copper deposited on the cathode, bubbles of oxygen at the anode, blue colour fades as Cu²⁺ is used. With copper electrodes the anode dissolves and the cathode grows (copper refining).

misconception.wrong: Electrons travel through the electrolyte to complete the circuit.
misconception.right: Electrons travel through the wires. In the electrolyte the circuit is completed by moving ions.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer D. Trap: pupils say sodium forms at the cathode. Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen is discharged.

check.q: What forms at the cathode when aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed?
check.why: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen ions are discharged at the cathode.

practice: Name the electrode where positive ions go.
Write the half-equation for copper ions at the cathode.
How do you test for chlorine?
independent: Core: Draw and label the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide.
Extend: Predict the products from dilute sulfuric acid with inert electrodes and write the half-equations. [4 marks]
Stretch: A student electrolyses copper(II) sulfate with copper electrodes. Describe and explain what happens to the electrodes. [4 marks]
exit: Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: explain how electricity pulls a metal from a liquid.

lessons.title: Group 1: the alkali metals
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is potassium kept under oil but gold can sit on a shelf for centuries?
objectives: Describe the physical properties and trends of Group 1
Describe reactions with water and air and write equations
Explain the trend in reactivity using electron structure
successCriteria: All: describe the reactions of lithium, sodium and potassium with water
Most: write equations and predict rubidium and caesium
Some: explain the reactivity trend using atomic structure
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: atomic size; Geography: alkali lakes
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: respect for hazards; trust in careful method (ihsan in the laboratory)

keywords.def: a Group 1 metal
how readily a substance reacts
inner electron shells reduce the nuclear attraction felt by the outer electron
compound containing OH⁻ ions, alkaline in water

starter: Bismillah. Write the electronic configuration of sodium.
What is the test for hydrogen gas?
Write the formula of sodium hydroxide.

teach.heading: Group 1 reactions with water
bullets: Metal floats, fizzes, moves and forms an alkaline solution
Lithium slow; sodium melts into a ball; potassium burns lilac
Hydrogen gas is made
teach.note: Teacher demonstration behind a safety screen with small pieces (rice-grain size). Pupils record observations. Equation: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. Universal indicator turns purple, pH 13 to 14. Never let pupils handle the metals.

head: Metal
Observations in water
Melting point (°C)
rows: melts to a ball, fizzes quickly, moves
very fast, lilac flame, may spark

teach.heading: Trends in the group
bullets: Softer and lower melting point down the group
More reactive down the group
Reaction with air: tarnish to oxide, stored under oil
teach.note: Ask pupils to extrapolate: predict the melting point of rubidium between 63 and 28 (about 39 in reality). Show: 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O. Group 1 compounds are white or colourless and dissolve in water.

model.problem: Predict how rubidium reacts with water and write the equation.
steps: Rubidium is below potassium, so more reactive
Reaction is more violent than potassium, with a flame or explosion
Products: rubidium hydroxide solution and hydrogen

teach.heading: Why reactivity increases
bullets: Group 1 atoms lose one outer electron
Larger atoms: outer electron is further from the nucleus
More shielding, weaker attraction, easier to lose
teach.note: This is the Chemistry-only electron explanation. Compare Li (2,1) with K (2,8,8,1). Pupils often say larger atoms have 'more electrons so more reactive'; the key idea is distance and shielding.

misconception.wrong: Potassium is more reactive because it has more electrons in its outer shell.
misconception.right: All Group 1 atoms have one outer electron. Potassium's is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: 'more electrons' or 'more protons' without distance and shielding.

check.q: Which statement best explains why caesium is more reactive than sodium?
options: Caesium's outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded
check.why: A bigger atom with more shielding holds its single outer electron less tightly, so it is lost more easily.

practice: Write the equation for lithium reacting with water.
Why are Group 1 metals stored under oil?
What colour does universal indicator turn in the solution?
independent: Core: Make a table of the reactions of Li, Na and K with water.
Extend: Predict and justify the melting point and reactivity of francium relative to caesium. [3 marks]
Stretch: Explain why the reaction of potassium with water produces a flame, referring to energy and hydrogen. [3 marks]
exit: State two trends going down Group 1. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: what does storage under oil tell us about the metal?
lessons.homework: Write a risk assessment for the sodium and water demonstration.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: video of the reactions with sentence frames. Stretch: explain flame colours.

lessons.title: Group 7: the halogens and displacement reactions
lessons.bigQuestion: Why can one halogen push another out of its compound?
objectives: Describe colour, state and trends of the halogens
Explain the trend in reactivity
Predict displacement reactions and write ionic equations
successCriteria: All: describe the colours and states
Most: predict displacement reactions
Some: write ionic equations and explain oxidation and reduction
lessons.crossCurricular: Health: disinfection of water; Industry: bleach
lessons.smsc: Moral: safe use of chemicals; protecting water supplies (public health)

keywords.def: Group 7 element
a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive one in a compound
made of molecules with two atoms, e.g. Cl₂
compound containing a halogen ion, e.g. Br⁻

starter: Bismillah. What type of bonding is in a chlorine molecule?
Write the charge on a chloride ion.
Define oxidation as loss of electrons.

teach.heading: Properties of the halogens
bullets: Diatomic non-metals
Melting and boiling points increase down the group
Colour gets darker down the group
teach.note: At room temperature: chlorine is a green gas, bromine a red-brown liquid, iodine a grey-black solid (purple vapour). Fluorine is a pale yellow gas, astatine a black solid (predicted). Chlorine and bromine are toxic; use only in a fume cupboard. Dissolved hydrogen halides such as HCl form acidic solutions.

teach.heading: Displacement reactions
bullets: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide
Reactivity decreases down the group
Colour changes show what is formed
teach.note: Practical: add chlorine water to potassium bromide and potassium iodide solutions (use dilute solutions and test tubes in a rack, teacher dispenses chlorine water). Results: bromide turns orange; iodide turns brown. Add bromine water to potassium iodide: brown. Reverse reactions do not happen.

teach.heading: Model: ionic equation
bullets: Write the full equation
Cancel spectator ions
Label oxidation and reduction
teach.note: Spectator ions (K⁺) appear on both sides. Chlorine gains electrons, so it is reduced; bromide ions lose electrons, so they are oxidised. Use OIL RIG.

model.problem: Chlorine is added to potassium bromide solution. Write the full and ionic equations.
model.answer: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂; chlorine is reduced and bromide is oxidised

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer D. Trap: pupils think any halogen displaces any halide; only a more reactive halogen can displace.

check.q: Which mixture produces a reaction?
check.why: Chlorine is more reactive than iodine, so it displaces it. In the other mixtures the added halogen is less reactive than the halide present.

practice: State the colour and state of bromine at room temperature.
Predict whether bromine displaces chlorine from sodium chloride. Explain.
Write the ionic equation for chlorine and potassium iodide.
independent: Core: Complete a table of the displacement results for chlorine, bromine and iodine.
Extend: Predict the properties of astatine and whether it displaces iodine from potassium iodide. [3 marks]
Stretch: Explain why reactivity falls down Group 7 but rises down Group 1. [4 marks]
exit: State the trend in boiling point down Group 7. [1 mark]
Return to the big question using the term more reactive.
lessons.homework: Create a flow chart to predict displacement results.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: colour swatches for observations. Stretch: explain reactivity of halogens in terms of electron capture.

lessons.title: Gases in air, carbonates and carbon dioxide
lessons.bigQuestion: What is air made of, and what happens when its carbon dioxide rises?
objectives: State the percentage composition of dry air
Describe how to find the percentage of oxygen in air
Describe thermal decomposition of metal carbonates and the greenhouse effect
successCriteria: All: state the composition of air
Most: calculate the percentage of oxygen from data
Some: explain the greenhouse effect and decomposition of carbonates
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: climate; Biology: photosynthesis
lessons.smsc: Stewardship (khilafah): responsibility for the atmosphere we share

keywords.def: breakdown of a compound by heating
gas that absorbs infrared radiation and warms the atmosphere
calcium hydroxide solution used to test for CO₂
proportion of each gas in a mixture

starter: Bismillah. Write the word equation for photosynthesis.
What is the test for carbon dioxide?
Name a fossil fuel.

teach.heading: Composition of dry air
bullets: Nitrogen about 78%
Oxygen about 21%
Argon about 0.9%, carbon dioxide about 0.04%
teach.note: Air is a mixture, so gases are not chemically combined. Water vapour is variable and is left out in dry air. Ask: which gas supports combustion? (oxygen) Which is unreactive? (nitrogen, argon).

teach.heading: Finding the oxygen content
bullets: Heat excess copper in a fixed volume of air
Copper reacts with the oxygen: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO
Measure the fall in gas volume
teach.note: Two gas syringes joined by a tube of hot copper turnings. Push the gas back and forth until the volume is constant, cool to room temperature, and read the final volume. Alternative: iron wool in a measuring cylinder over water.

model.problem: 80 cm³ of air is passed over hot copper until the volume is constant at 63 cm³. Calculate the percentage of oxygen.

teach.heading: Metal carbonates and carbon dioxide
bullets: Copper(II) carbonate: green to black on heating
CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂
Test for CO₂: limewater turns milky
teach.note: Practical: heat copper(II) carbonate in a boiling tube with a delivery tube into limewater. Ask what the colour change tells us. Group 1 carbonates (except lithium) do not decompose at Bunsen temperatures.

teach.heading: Greenhouse effect
bullets: CO₂ and methane absorb infrared radiation from Earth
Some is re-emitted back to Earth, warming the atmosphere
CO₂ was about 280 ppm before industry and is above 420 ppm today
teach.note: Be accurate and neutral: the greenhouse effect is natural and keeps Earth habitable. The enhanced effect arises from the increased amounts of greenhouse gases. Sources: burning fossil fuels, deforestation. Sinks: photosynthesis, oceans.

misconception.wrong: The greenhouse effect is the same thing as the hole in the ozone layer.
misconception.right: They are separate: the greenhouse effect involves infrared radiation absorbed by gases such as CO₂ and methane.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: a green-to-black colour change alone does not identify the gas; the limewater test does.

check.q: Which observation shows carbon dioxide is released when copper(II) carbonate is heated?
options: The solid turns from green to black
A gas bubbles through the liquid
check.why: The limewater test is specific to carbon dioxide. A colour change shows a new substance formed but not which gas.

practice: State the percentage of nitrogen and of argon in air.
Write the equation for the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate.
Name two sources of carbon dioxide.
independent: Core: In an experiment 100 cm³ of air falls to 79 cm³. Calculate the percentage of oxygen.
Extend: Explain why the apparatus must be cooled before the final volume is read. [2 marks]
Stretch: Explain how the greenhouse effect warms the Earth. [4 marks]
exit: Give the test and positive result for carbon dioxide. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: describe both the composition of air and the effect of CO₂.
lessons.homework: Draw a pie chart of the composition of air and write three sentences on the greenhouse effect.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: test and result cards. Stretch: why is argon used in lamps?

lessons.title: The reactivity series, rusting and redox
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does iron rust but gold stay shiny, and how can zinc save a ship?
objectives: Order metals by reactivity from reactions with water, acid and displacement
Describe rusting and rust prevention
Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons and oxygen
successCriteria: All: recall the reactivity order
Most: predict displacement and describe rusting
Some: write ionic equations and identify oxidising and reducing agents
lessons.crossCurricular: Engineering: corrosion; History: iron and bronze ages
lessons.smsc: Stewardship: making things last reduces waste

keywords.def: list of metals in order of reactivity
more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in a compound
loss of electrons (or gain of oxygen)
protecting iron by attaching a more reactive metal that corrodes instead

starter: Bismillah. Name two metals that react with cold water.
Write the equation for magnesium burning in oxygen.
What does 'ion' mean?

teach.heading: Ordering metals
bullets: Observe reactions with water and dilute acid
Displacement shows relative reactivity
Order: K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, (C), Zn, Fe, (H), Cu, Ag, Au
teach.note: Practical: add small pieces of Mg, Zn, Fe and Cu to dilute hydrochloric acid and record the bubbling rate. Magnesium is most vigorous, zinc moderate, iron slow, copper no reaction. Gold is found as the element. Reactivity series teaches 'who wins' in displacement.

teach.heading: Displacement and redox
bullets: Mg + CuSO₄ → MgSO₄ + Cu
Ionic: Mg + Cu²⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Cu
Mg loses electrons (oxidised); Cu²⁺ gains (reduced)
teach.note: Observations: blue colour fades, brown copper solid, temperature rises. A reaction with both oxidation and reduction is a redox reaction. Oxidising agent gains electrons (Cu²⁺); reducing agent loses electrons (Mg).

model.problem: Zinc is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. Write the ionic equation and identify what is oxidised.
steps: Zinc is more reactive than copper so it displaces it
Zinc is oxidised; Cu²⁺ is reduced
model.answer: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu; zinc is oxidised

teach.heading: Rusting and prevention
bullets: Iron + oxygen + water → hydrated iron(III) oxide
Both air and water are needed
Salt speeds up rusting
teach.note: Experiment: nails in four tubes: dry (calcium chloride), boiled water with oil, air and water, salt water. Only the last two rust, and salt water rusts fastest. Prevention: barrier (paint, oil, plastic), galvanising (zinc coat), sacrificial protection (magnesium or zinc blocks on ship hulls). Tin plating protects only while unscratched; zinc continues to protect even when scratched.

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils confuse sacrificial protection with a barrier layer.

check.q: Why is a block of magnesium bolted to a steel ship hull?
options: It is more reactive than iron so it corrodes instead
It is less reactive than iron
check.why: Magnesium is more reactive than iron, so it loses electrons and corrodes first, protecting the iron.

practice: List four metals in order of reactivity.
Write the word equation for rusting.
Predict whether copper displaces zinc from zinc sulfate.
independent: Core: Complete a table of predicted displacement results for Mg, Zn, Fe and Cu with their sulfates.
Extend: Write ionic equations for iron with copper sulfate and label oxidation and reduction. [3 marks]
Stretch: Explain why zinc coating still protects scratched iron but tin does not. [3 marks]
exit: Define oxidation in terms of electrons. [1 mark]
Return to the big question: explain sacrificial protection.
lessons.homework: Revise the series and design a poster on rust prevention.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: colour-coded series with a mnemonic. Stretch: why does aluminium resist corrosion despite being reactive?

lessons.title: Extracting metals, uses and alloys
lessons.bigQuestion: Why was iron used for thousands of years before aluminium became common?
objectives: Link the method of extraction to the position in the reactivity series
Describe the extraction of iron and aluminium
State uses of metals and alloys and explain alloy properties
successCriteria: All: link method to reactivity
Most: describe the blast furnace and electrolysis of aluminium oxide
Some: explain alloy hardness and evaluate recycling
lessons.crossCurricular: Engineering: materials; Economics: energy costs
lessons.smsc: Stewardship: recycling metals and avoiding waste

keywords.def: rock containing enough metal to be extracted profitably
loss of oxygen (or gain of electrons)
mixture of a metal with other elements
compound used to lower the melting point of aluminium oxide

starter: Bismillah. State the order of reactivity of Mg, Fe, Cu and C.
What is the cathode?
Define oxidation and reduction.

teach.heading: Method follows reactivity
bullets: Unreactive metals: found native or heated
Metals less reactive than carbon: reduce with carbon
Metals more reactive than carbon: electrolysis
teach.note: Remind pupils of the series. Gold is found uncombined; iron oxide is reduced by carbon; aluminium oxide needs electrolysis because aluminium holds oxygen more strongly than carbon does.

teach.heading: The blast furnace
bullets: Carbon burns to make heat and carbon monoxide
Carbon monoxide reduces iron(III) oxide
Limestone removes sand as slag
teach.note: Equations: C + O₂ → CO₂; CO₂ + C → 2CO; Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂; CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂; CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ (slag). Molten iron sinks, slag floats on top.

model.problem: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. State what is reduced and what is oxidised.
steps: Iron(III) oxide loses oxygen, so it is reduced
Carbon monoxide gains oxygen to form CO₂, so it is oxidised
model.answer: Fe₂O₃ is reduced; CO is oxidised

teach.heading: Aluminium by electrolysis
bullets: Bauxite purified to aluminium oxide
Dissolved in molten cryolite at about 950 °C
Cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al
Anode: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻
teach.note: Cryolite lowers the temperature from about 2000 °C, saving energy. The oxygen reacts with the hot carbon anodes to make CO₂, so the anodes burn away and must be replaced. Recycling aluminium uses about 5% of the energy of making new metal.

right.title: Alloys
points: Brass (Cu + Zn); steel (Fe + C); stainless steel

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer D. Trap: pupils say zinc needs electrolysis because it is reactive; it is below carbon so carbon works.

check.q: Which metal is extracted from its oxide by electrolysis?
check.why: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon. Iron, zinc and copper can be reduced using carbon.

practice: Why is cryolite used in the extraction of aluminium?
Explain why aluminium cannot be extracted by heating with carbon.
Give one use of brass and one of stainless steel.
independent: Core: Draw a flow chart for extracting iron in the blast furnace.
Extend: Explain why carbon anodes need replacing in aluminium extraction. [2 marks]
Stretch: Evaluate the claim that recycling aluminium is always better than extracting it. [4 marks]
exit: Name the method used for a metal above carbon in the reactivity series. [1 mark]
Return to the big question: explain the order of discovery.
lessons.homework: Revision card: methods of extraction for iron, aluminium and gold.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: labelled blast-furnace diagram. Stretch: why does steel contain carbon?

lessons.title: Acids, alkalis, pH, indicators and titration
lessons.bigQuestion: How can you measure exactly how much acid is needed to neutralise an alkali?
objectives: Describe the pH scale and common indicators
Write the neutralisation reaction as H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O
Describe a titration and calculate an unknown concentration
successCriteria: All: use the pH scale and indicators
Most: describe titration
Some: calculate concentration from titration results
lessons.crossCurricular: Biology: pH and enzymes; Home: antacids
lessons.smsc: Moral: precision and honesty in results

keywords.def: soluble base that forms OH⁻ ions in water
scale of 0 to 14 measuring acidity
reaction of an acid with a base to form a salt and water
volume of solution added from a burette

starter: Bismillah. Name the acid in the stomach.
Write the formula for hydrochloric acid.
Convert 21.4 cm³ to dm³.

teach.heading: pH and indicators
bullets: pH below 7 acid, 7 neutral, above 7 alkaline
Universal indicator gives a range of colours
Litmus, methyl orange, phenolphthalein show end points
teach.note: Colour table below. Universal indicator: red (strong acid) to violet (strong alkali). An acid produces H⁺ ions in water; an alkali produces OH⁻ ions.

teach.heading: Neutralisation
bullets: Acid + alkali → salt + water
Ionic equation: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)
HCl gives chlorides, H₂SO₄ sulfates, HNO₃ nitrates
teach.note: Write NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O. Neutralisation is exothermic. Point out the spectator ions (Na⁺, Cl⁻).
cycle: Pipette 25.0 cm³ of alkali into a flask
Add acid until the colour just changes

teach.heading: Model: titration calculation
bullets: moles of acid = concentration × volume (dm³)
Use the 1:1 ratio
Concentration of alkali = moles ÷ 25.0 cm³ in dm³
teach.note: Method points: rinse apparatus with the solutions to be used, read the burette at eye level to the bottom of the meniscus, add dropwise near the end point, concordant results within 0.10 cm³. Titres 21.45, 21.40, 21.35 give mean 21.40 cm³.

model.problem: 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide needs a mean of 21.40 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH.
steps: Ratio HCl : NaOH = 1 : 1, so n(NaOH) = 0.00214 mol

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: universal indicator changes colour gradually, so it is poor for finding a sharp end point.

check.q: Which indicator is most suitable for finding the end point of a titration?
check.why: Methyl orange gives a sharp colour change at the end point. Universal indicator and pH paper change gradually.

practice: Give the colour of methyl orange in acid and in alkali.
Write the ionic equation for neutralisation.
Calculate the moles in 18.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ acid.
independent: Core: Explain how to carry out a titration using a burette and pipette.
Extend: 25.0 cm³ of KOH needs 18.50 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ HCl. Calculate the concentration of KOH. [3 marks]
Stretch: 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide reacts with sulfuric acid in a 2:1 ratio. Mean titre 12.50 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ H₂SO₄. Calculate the NaOH concentration. [4 marks]
exit: State why concordant results are needed. [1 mark]
Return to the big question: summarise how you know how much acid is enough.
lessons.homework: Practise two titration calculations and describe the method in order.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: method step cards. Stretch: strong versus weak acids.

lessons.title: Acids and bases as proton transfer; preparing salts
lessons.bigQuestion: How do you make a pure blue crystal from a black powder?
objectives: Apply solubility rules to common salts
Describe acids as proton donors and bases as proton acceptors
Describe preparing soluble salts and insoluble salts
successCriteria: All: use solubility rules
Most: describe how to make copper(II) sulfate crystals
Some: choose a method for any salt and write ionic equations
lessons.crossCurricular: Industry: fertilisers; Geography: mineral deposits
lessons.smsc: Moral: safe handling of toxic substances such as lead compounds

keywords.def: species that gives H⁺: an acid
species that accepts H⁺: a base
insoluble solid formed in a reaction between solutions
form crystals as a solution cools or evaporates

starter: Bismillah. Write the equation for neutralisation of HCl with NaOH.
State the formula of sulfuric acid.
What is filtration?

teach.heading: Solubility rules and proton transfer
bullets: All nitrates, and sodium, potassium and ammonium salts, are soluble
Chlorides soluble except silver and lead
Sulfates soluble except lead, barium and calcium
teach.note: Carbonates and hydroxides are insoluble except those of sodium, potassium and ammonium. In HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻, HCl donates a proton, so is an acid. NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺, ammonia accepts a proton, so is a base.

teach.heading: Making a soluble salt: copper(II) sulfate
bullets: Warm dilute sulfuric acid
Add excess copper(II) oxide, stirring
Filter off the excess solid
Evaporate partially and crystallise
teach.note: Equation: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O. Excess black copper oxide ensures all acid reacts; the unreacted solid is filtered. Heat the filtrate until a drop on a glass rod crystallises, then leave to cool. Dry the crystals between filter papers. Safety: goggles; do not boil dry. For an alkali plus acid a titration is needed to find the exact amounts, then repeat without indicator.

teach.heading: Model: choose a method
bullets: Is the salt soluble or insoluble?
Soluble: acid + metal, base or carbonate
Insoluble: precipitation by mixing solutions
teach.note: Example: lead(II) sulfate. Mix lead(II) nitrate and sodium sulfate solutions: Pb(NO₃)₂ + Na₂SO₄ → PbSO₄ + 2NaNO₃. Ionic: Pb²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → PbSO₄(s). Filter, wash with distilled water, dry in a warm oven. Lead compounds are toxic: wear gloves, wash hands.

model.problem: Describe how to make a pure, dry sample of barium sulfate.
steps: Barium sulfate is insoluble, so use precipitation
Mix barium chloride solution with sodium sulfate solution
Filter to collect the solid and wash with distilled water

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer B. Trap: pupils pick evaporation for a salt that is insoluble.

check.q: Which method makes a pure sample of zinc sulfate crystals?
options: Mix zinc nitrate and sodium sulfate
Add excess zinc oxide to dilute sulfuric acid, filter, crystallise
check.why: Zinc sulfate is soluble, so react zinc oxide with sulfuric acid in excess, filter, then crystallise.

practice: State two soluble and two insoluble salts.
Why is excess copper oxide added in the preparation?
Write the ionic equation for the formation of lead(II) sulfate.
independent: Core: Describe how to make sodium chloride crystals from sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid.
Extend: Use solubility rules to predict if a precipitate forms when silver nitrate is mixed with sodium chloride. Write the ionic equation. [3 marks]
Stretch: Explain, with a proton-transfer equation, why ammonia is a base. [2 marks]
exit: Name two methods of making salts and when each is used. [2 marks]
Return to the big question: what makes the blue crystal appear?
lessons.homework: Write a risk assessment and method for making a salt of your choice.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: method cards in order. Stretch: why is ammonium nitrate a good fertiliser?
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Biology 4BI1, Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1; Science (Double Award) 4SD0

lessons.title: Identifying gases, ions and water
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a chemist identify an unknown substance without tasting or guessing?
objectives: Describe tests for common gases and for water
Carry out flame tests and tests for cations
Describe tests for halides, sulfate and carbonate
successCriteria: All: recall gas tests
Most: identify cations and anions from observations
Some: deduce the identity of an unknown from several results
lessons.crossCurricular: Forensic science; Biology: testing water quality
lessons.smsc: Moral: truthfulness in evidence; careful and ethical observation

keywords.def: test for metal ions using the colour a compound gives a flame
insoluble solid formed in a solution
negative ion
positive ion

starter: Bismillah. What is the test for oxygen?
Write the formula of the sulfate ion.
What is a precipitate?

teach.heading: Gases and water
bullets: H₂: lit splint, squeaky pop
O₂: glowing splint relights
CO₂: limewater milky; Cl₂: damp litmus bleached; NH₃: damp red litmus blue
teach.note: Water: anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns from white to blue; cobalt chloride paper turns blue to pink. Pure water boils at 100 °C and freezes at 0 °C at standard pressure. These tests check for water, but only the boiling point shows purity.

teach.heading: Cations
bullets: Flame: Li⁺ red, Na⁺ yellow, K⁺ lilac, Cu²⁺ blue-green
Add NaOH: Cu²⁺ blue, Fe²⁺ green, Fe³⁺ red-brown precipitate
NH₄⁺: warm with NaOH, ammonia turns damp litmus blue
teach.note: Flame test method: clean a nichrome wire in acid, dip in the sample, hold in a blue Bunsen flame. Calcium gives orange-red. The precipitate colours below are the key evidence.

teach.heading: Anions
bullets: Halides: add dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate
Sulfate: add dilute HCl then barium chloride, white precipitate
Carbonate: add dilute acid, effervescence, CO₂ turns limewater milky
teach.note: Halide colours: chloride white, bromide cream, iodide yellow. The acid is added first to remove carbonates and hydroxides that would interfere.

model.problem: A white solid gives a lilac flame. A solution of it with dilute HCl and barium chloride gives a white precipitate. Identify the compound.
steps: White precipitate with HCl and BaCl₂ means sulfate ions

teach.heading: Hinge question
bullets: Answer on mini-whiteboards
teach.note: Answer C. Trap: pupils say 'blue' for any copper test; both the flame colour and hydroxide precipitate are different.

check.q: A solution forms a green precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution. Which ion is present?
check.why: Fe²⁺ gives a green precipitate. Cu²⁺ gives blue and Fe³⁺ gives red-brown.

practice: Give the test and result for hydrogen.
State the flame colour of lithium and of potassium ions.
Why is dilute nitric acid added before silver nitrate?
independent: Core: Complete a table of tests for chloride, bromide, iodide, sulfate and carbonate.
Extend: Tube A gives a yellow precipitate with silver nitrate and nitric acid. A flame test gives yellow. Identify the compound. [3 marks]
Stretch: Design a plan to identify an unlabelled white solid that could be calcium carbonate or sodium chloride. [4 marks]
exit: Give the test for water. [1 mark]
Return to the big question: choose one unknown and explain how you would identify it.
lessons.homework: Make a test summary sheet (one table: cations, anions, gases).
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: colour cards and a decision tree. Stretch: ethical reasons for evidence in testing.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Biology 4BI1, Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1; Science (Double Award) 4SD0

lessons.title: Vectors, scalars and resultant forces in two dimensions
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a runner who completes a 400 m lap have a distance of 400 m but a displacement of zero?
objectives: Distinguish vector from scalar quantities and give SI units
Calculate the resultant of two perpendicular forces
Use a scale drawing to find a resultant
successCriteria: All: classify quantities as vector or scalar
Most: find a resultant of two perpendicular forces by Pythagoras
Some: find its direction using trigonometry or a scale drawing
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: Pythagoras, trigonometry and scale drawing
lessons.smsc: Moral: precision in measurement and honest reporting of results

keywords.def: a quantity with magnitude (size) only
a quantity with magnitude and direction
distance in a straight line from start to finish, with direction
the single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting together

starter: Bismillah. State the SI unit of force, mass, time and energy.
A car travels 90 km in 1.5 hours. Calculate its average speed in km/h.
A 4 kg trolley has a resultant force of 12 N. Calculate its acceleration.

teach.heading: Scalars and vectors
bullets: Scalar: size only, e.g. mass, distance, speed, time, energy
Vector: size and direction, e.g. force, velocity, displacement
Vectors are drawn as arrows: length shows size
teach.note: Ask pupils to sort ten quantities onto mini-whiteboards. Recall SI base units here: metre, kilogram, second; newton (N) and joule (J) are derived units. Stress that in one dimension direction can be shown by a sign (+/-).

teach.heading: Forces at right angles
bullets: Forces that do not line up cannot simply be added
For perpendicular forces use Pythagoras: R² = F₁² + F₂²
Direction: tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent
teach.note: Draw the force triangle head-to-tail on the board. Walk through why 6 N and 8 N do not make 14 N. Show that a scale drawing (1 cm = 1 kN) gives the same answer, as examiners may ask for either method.

model.problem: Two tugboats pull a ship. One pulls 6.0 kN due east, the other 8.0 kN due north. Find the size and direction of the resultant.
steps: Draw the forces head to tail as a right-angled triangle
tan θ = 8.0 ÷ 6.0 = 1.33, so θ = 53° north of east
model.answer: Resultant = 10 kN at 53° north of east

teach.heading: Distance and displacement
bullets: Distance is how far you travelled along the path
Displacement is the straight-line distance from the start, with direction
Speed is a scalar; velocity is a vector
teach.note: Return to the big question: a full lap gives displacement 0, so average velocity is 0 even though average speed is not. Ask: can an object move at constant speed but changing velocity? (Yes: circular motion.)

misconception.wrong: A negative velocity means the object is slowing down.
misconception.right: A negative velocity only means the direction is opposite to the one chosen as positive. Slowing down means the acceleration is opposite to the velocity.

teach.heading: Check: scalar or vector?
bullets: Decide, then show your whiteboards
teach.note: Hinge question. Pupils choosing B are thinking only of size. Pupils choosing C or D have mixed up vectors and scalars, for example thinking weight and mass are the same.

check.q: Which list contains only vector quantities?
check.why: Force, displacement and acceleration all have direction. Speed (B, D), mass, time, energy and distance are scalars.

practice: A boat is pushed 9 N east by the engine and 12 N north by the current. Calculate the size of the resultant force.
A hiker walks 3 km east then 4 km north. State her distance and her displacement.
Draw a scale diagram (1 cm = 2 N) to find the resultant of 10 N west and 4 N south.
independent: Core: Classify each as scalar or vector: temperature, momentum, volume, acceleration, speed, displacement.
Extend: Forces of 5.0 N and 12 N act at right angles on a 2.0 kg trolley. Calculate the resultant and the magnitude of the acceleration.
Stretch: A swimmer aims directly across a 60 m wide river at 1.5 m/s. The river flows at 2.0 m/s. Calculate the swimmer's resultant speed and how far downstream she lands.
exit: Explain the difference between speed and velocity.
A force of 3 N and a force of 4 N act at right angles. Show that the resultant is 5 N.
lessons.homework: Find three everyday situations where two forces act at an angle and write one sentence about each. Then complete five resultant-force calculations from the worksheet.
lessons.send: SEND: give a pre-drawn right-angled triangle template and a Pythagoras triples card (3-4-5, 5-12-13). EAL: pair 'scalar' and 'vector' with drawn arrows. Stretch: resolve a force into horizontal and vertical components.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Biology 4BI1, Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1; Science (Double Award) 4SD0

lessons.title: Falling objects, drag and terminal velocity
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a skydiver stop speeding up even though gravity never switches off?
objectives: Describe the forces on a falling object
Explain terminal velocity in terms of balanced forces
Interpret a velocity-time graph for a skydiver
successCriteria: All: state that terminal velocity is reached when forces balance
Most: explain each stage of a skydive using resultant force
Some: calculate acceleration at a given instant from weight and drag
lessons.crossCurricular: PE/Geography: skydiving; DT: parachute shapes
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at the laws that govern ordinary things

keywords.def: resistive force on an object moving through a fluid, such as air resistance
the constant maximum speed reached when drag equals the driving force
the force of gravity on an object, W = mg
the overall force after adding forces with direction

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the weight of a 60 kg person (g = 10 N/kg).
State Newton's second law as an equation.
Describe a velocity-time graph showing constant acceleration.

teach.heading: Two forces on a falling object
bullets: Weight acts downwards and stays constant
Drag acts upwards and increases with speed
Resultant force = weight - drag
teach.note: Begin with a coin dropped in air: it feels weight and a very small drag. Ask pupils how drag would differ for a feather. Emphasise that weight does not change as the object falls, but drag does.
cycle: Start: speed zero, drag zero, resultant = weight
Speed rises, drag rises, acceleration falls
Resultant force zero: constant speed (terminal velocity)

teach.heading: Worked example: the skydiver
bullets: Mass 80 kg; use g = 10 N/kg
Find weight, resultant and acceleration when drag is 300 N
Find drag at terminal velocity
teach.note: Model aloud: always draw a free-body diagram first, label weight down and drag up. Note that at terminal velocity the object still moves; it just stops accelerating.

model.problem: An 80 kg skydiver falls. At one instant drag is 300 N. Calculate his acceleration. What is the drag at terminal velocity?
steps: At terminal velocity the resultant is zero, so drag = weight = 800 N
model.answer: a = 6.25 m/s² downwards; drag at terminal velocity = 800 N

teach.heading: The skydive on a velocity-time graph
bullets: Steep curve: large acceleration at the start
Curve flattens as drag grows
Horizontal line: terminal velocity
Parachute opens: speed drops, then a lower terminal velocity
teach.note: Sketch the graph live. Ask: what does the gradient show at each point? Why does opening the parachute make the resultant force point upwards for a moment? The numbers on the timeline are illustrative, not exact.

timeline.label: Chute opens
timeline.text: Drag greater than weight, slows down

teach.heading: Common errors
bullets: Heavier does not always mean faster in air
In a vacuum all objects fall with the same acceleration
Terminal velocity depends on shape and area as well as weight
teach.note: Mention the Apollo 15 hammer and feather demonstration on the Moon (1971). Contrast with a feather and coin in air. Link back: a = F/m, so a heavier object has more weight but also more mass.

misconception.wrong: At terminal velocity there are no forces acting on the object.
misconception.right: At terminal velocity two forces act, weight and drag, but they are equal and opposite, so the resultant force is zero.

teach.heading: Check: balanced forces
bullets: Choose the best statement
teach.note: Distractor A is the classic misconception that gravity stops. B has the forces the wrong way round. D confuses constant speed with no drag.

check.q: A parachutist falls at constant speed. Which statement is correct?
check.why: Constant speed means zero resultant force, so drag equals weight. Gravity always acts (A) and drag is not zero (D).

practice: A 0.050 kg ball bearing is dropped in oil. Weight is 0.50 N and drag is 0.20 N. Calculate the resultant force and acceleration.
Explain why a skydiver reaches a higher terminal velocity falling head-first than spread out.
A 70 kg parachutist falls at terminal velocity. State the drag force.
independent: Core: Describe in order the forces and motion of a skydiver from jumping to landing with a parachute.
Extend: Sketch a velocity-time graph for a parachutist who opens the parachute at 10 s. Label the terminal velocities and explain each section.
Stretch: Explain, using resultant force, why a raindrop falling from a high cloud does not hit the ground at very high speed.
exit: Define terminal velocity.
A 60 kg skydiver has drag 450 N. Calculate the acceleration (g = 10 N/kg).
lessons.homework: Design a parachute test using coffee filters: list the independent, dependent and control variables and one safety point.
lessons.send: SEND: provide the four-stage cycle as a card sort and a labelled free-body diagram. EAL: pre-teach drag, resistive, constant. Stretch: explain why terminal velocity depends on cross-sectional area.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Biology 4BI1, Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1; Science (Double Award) 4SD0

lessons.title: Momentum and the conservation of momentum
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a small bullet fired from a gun make the gun kick back?
objectives: Calculate momentum using p = mv
State and apply the conservation of momentum in collisions and explosions
successCriteria: All: calculate momentum
Most: use conservation of momentum for two objects sticking together
Some: solve explosion and recoil problems
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: rearranging equations; PE: collisions in rugby
lessons.smsc: Moral: responsibility for the safe handling of equipment

keywords.def: mass multiplied by velocity, a vector measured in kg m/s
total momentum before = total momentum after, if no external force acts
two objects interacting briefly with large forces
objects pushed apart from rest

starter: Bismillah. A 1500 kg car moves at 20 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.
Which of these is a vector: speed, mass, velocity?
State Newton's first law.

teach.heading: Momentum
bullets: p = m × v
Unit: kg m/s
Vector: direction matters, so choose a positive direction
teach.note: Compare a lorry and a cyclist at the same speed. Pupils feel why the lorry is harder to stop. Emphasise that momentum has the direction of velocity, so +/- signs are essential.

model.problem: Calculate the momentum of a 1200 kg car moving at 15 m/s, and of a 0.15 kg cricket ball at 30 m/s.
steps: Same formula; unit is kg m/s
model.answer: Car 18 000 kg m/s; ball 4.5 kg m/s

teach.heading: Conservation of momentum
bullets: In a closed system, total momentum before = total momentum after
Applies to all collisions and explosions
Kinetic energy may not be conserved (inelastic collision)
teach.note: Use trolleys on a track with light gates if available. Method: 1) choose a positive direction, 2) write total p before, 3) write total p after, 4) equate. 'Closed' means no external forces such as friction.

model.problem: A 2.0 kg trolley moving at 3.0 m/s collides with a stationary 1.0 kg trolley. They stick together. Find their common velocity.
model.answer: Common velocity = 2.0 m/s in the original direction

teach.heading: Explosions and recoil
bullets: Before: at rest, so total momentum = 0
After: momenta equal in size and opposite in direction
The lighter object gets the higher speed
teach.note: Demonstrate with two spring-loaded trolleys pushed apart. Ask why the bullet gets a much greater speed than the gun: the momenta are equal and opposite, the bullet has far less mass, so its velocity is greater.

model.problem: A 4.0 kg rifle fires a 0.010 kg bullet at 400 m/s. Find the recoil velocity of the rifle.
steps: Rifle: 4.0 × v = -4.0 so that the total is 0
model.answer: Rifle recoils at 1.0 m/s opposite to the bullet

teach.heading: Check: collision
bullets: Use conservation of momentum
teach.note: Distractor A forgets the extra mass. C multiplies instead of conserving. Ask pupils to show their working on whiteboards.

check.q: A 3 kg trolley at 4 m/s hits and sticks to a stationary 1 kg trolley. What is the speed after?
check.why: Momentum before = 12 kg m/s. After: 4 kg × v = 12, so v = 3 m/s. A ignores the extra mass.

practice: Calculate the momentum of a 65 kg runner at 8.0 m/s.
A 0.50 kg trolley at 2.0 m/s hits a stationary 1.5 kg trolley and they stick together. Calculate their velocity.
A 60 kg skater at rest throws a 2 kg ball at 6 m/s. Calculate the skater's recoil velocity.
independent: Core: A 1000 kg car at 12 m/s hits a stationary 800 kg car and they lock together. Find the velocity after.
Extend: A 2 kg trolley moves right at 5 m/s and collides with a 3 kg trolley moving left at 2 m/s. They stick together. Find the velocity.
Stretch: A 0.20 kg ball at 6 m/s hits a 0.80 kg stationary ball, which moves off at 2.0 m/s. Find the velocity of the first ball and decide whether kinetic energy was conserved.
exit: State the principle of conservation of momentum.
A 5 kg cannon fires a 0.5 kg shell at 40 m/s. Calculate the cannon's recoil velocity.
lessons.homework: Write a half-page explanation of why a bullet gets a larger velocity than the gun, using the word 'momentum' at least four times.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a before/after momentum table for each object. EAL: sentence frames 'The momentum before is...'. Stretch: consider why kinetic energy is lost in sticking collisions.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Biology 4BI1, Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1; Science (Double Award) 4SD0

lessons.title: Force as rate of change of momentum; Newton's third law
lessons.bigQuestion: How do crumple zones and airbags protect the people inside a car?
objectives: Use F = (mv - mu) ÷ t
Explain safety features in terms of change of momentum
State and apply Newton's third law
successCriteria: All: state Newton's third law
Most: calculate force from change in momentum and time
Some: explain safety features and identify third-law pairs correctly
lessons.crossCurricular: Engineering: vehicle safety; Maths: substitution and rearranging
lessons.smsc: Moral: protecting human life through careful design

keywords.def: change in momentum, equal to force × time
change in momentum divided by time taken, equal to force
when A pushes on B, B pushes on A with an equal and opposite force
part of a car designed to collapse and lengthen the collision time

starter: Bismillah. A 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s has what momentum?
A 5 kg object has a resultant force of 20 N. Find its acceleration.
State the unit of momentum.

teach.heading: Force as rate of change of momentum
bullets: Newton's second law: F = Δp ÷ t
F = (mv - mu) ÷ t
Longer time means smaller force for the same change in momentum
teach.note: Link to F = ma: substitute a = (v - u)/t into F = ma and show it matches. Pupils practise on whiteboards with simple numbers first.

model.problem: A 1200 kg car travelling at 20 m/s stops in 0.80 s in a crash. Calculate the average force on the car. Repeat for 2.0 s.
steps: F = Δp ÷ t = 24 000 ÷ 0.80 = 30 000 N (opposing the motion)

teach.heading: Safety features
bullets: Crumple zones, airbags and seat belts increase the stopping time
Same change in momentum, so smaller force
Smaller force means less injury
Gymnastics mats and cycle helmets work in the same way
teach.note: Ask pupils to explain crumple zones in a three-part sentence: increases time, reduces rate of change of momentum, so force is smaller. Use a raw egg dropped onto a pillow versus the floor as a thought experiment.

head: Feature
How it helps
rows: slows the head over a longer time and spreads the force
stretches slightly and stops the body with the car

teach.heading: Newton's third law
bullets: Forces always come in pairs between two objects
Equal in size, opposite in direction, same type of force
The pair act on different objects
teach.note: Use the example of a book on a table. The Earth pulling the book down pairs with the book pulling the Earth up, not with the contact force from the table. Ask pupils to name the pair for a rocket and for a swimmer pushing off the wall.

misconception.wrong: The two forces in a third-law pair cancel out, so nothing can ever move.
misconception.right: The forces act on different objects so they cannot cancel. A swimmer pushes the wall; the wall pushes the swimmer, who accelerates.

teach.heading: Check: crash force
bullets: Think about time and momentum
teach.note: A and D wrongly say momentum or mass changes. C is the opposite of the real effect.

check.q: A cyclist's helmet reduces injury because it...
options: increases the time taken to stop, reducing force
check.why: The change in momentum is fixed, so a longer stopping time gives a smaller force. The helmet does not change momentum or mass.

practice: A 0.057 kg tennis ball hits a racket at 40 m/s and leaves at 20 m/s in the opposite direction in 0.0050 s. Calculate the average force on the ball.
A 70 kg driver at 15 m/s is stopped by a seat belt in 0.30 s. Calculate the force.
Identify the third-law pair when a footballer kicks a ball.
independent: Core: Explain why a long jumper bends their knees on landing.
Extend: A 0.40 kg ball falls onto a floor at 6 m/s and rebounds at 4 m/s. Contact time is 0.020 s. Calculate the average force on the ball.
Stretch: A hose sprays 2.0 kg of water per second at 8 m/s on to a wall and stops it. Calculate the force on the wall.
exit: Show that a force of 24 N is needed to change the momentum of a trolley by 12 kg m/s in 0.50 s.
State the third-law partner of the Earth's pull on you.
lessons.homework: Write a short advert for a child car seat explaining, using momentum, why it is safer than a rigid seat.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence frame 'Same change in momentum, longer time, so smaller force'. EAL: pre-teach crumple, rebound. Stretch: derive F = Δp/t from F = ma.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Biology 4BI1, Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1; Science (Double Award) 4SD0

lessons.title: Moments, centre of gravity and the principle of moments
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a small child balance an adult on a seesaw?
objectives: Calculate the moment of a force
Apply the principle of moments to a balanced object
Find the centre of gravity of a lamina and explain stability
successCriteria: All: calculate a moment
Most: use the principle of moments to find an unknown force or distance
Some: use a non-central pivot including the weight of a uniform beam
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: rearranging equations; DT: levers and tools; PE: balance
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: balance and proportion in nature and in life

keywords.def: turning effect of a force: force × perpendicular distance from the pivot
the point about which an object turns
for balance, total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment
the point where the whole weight of an object seems to act

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the weight of a 40 kg child (g = 10 N/kg).
State the unit of force.
Explain what a resultant force of zero means for an object.

teach.heading: The moment of a force
bullets: Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot
Unit: newton metre (N m)
A longer spanner gives a larger moment for the same force
teach.note: Demonstrate with a door: push near the hinge, then near the handle. Stress 'perpendicular' distance and convert cm to m before calculating.

model.problem: A mechanic pushes with 80 N on a spanner at 0.25 m from the nut. Find the moment. What force is needed at 0.40 m for the same moment?
steps: Same moment at 0.40 m: F = M ÷ d

teach.heading: The principle of moments
bullets: Balanced: clockwise moments = anticlockwise moments
The resultant moment is zero
Take moments about the pivot
teach.note: Practical: balance a metre rule on a pivot using 100 g masses; record the distances; check that W1 × d1 = W2 × d2 within experimental error. Independent variable: position of one mass; dependent: position of the other that balances. Safety: keep feet clear of falling masses.

model.problem: A child weighs 300 N and sits 2.0 m from the pivot of a seesaw. An adult weighs 600 N. Where must the adult sit to balance it?
model.answer: The adult sits 1.0 m from the pivot on the opposite side

teach.heading: Centre of gravity of a lamina
bullets: Centre of gravity: the point where the weight seems to act
Hang the lamina from a pin, with a plumb line
Mark the vertical line, repeat from two more holes
The lines cross at the centre of gravity
teach.note: Do the plumb-line practical in pairs. The lamina hangs freely so its centre of gravity ends directly below the pin. Safety: care with pins and loose plumb bobs. Three lines should cross at one point; a small triangle shows measurement error.
cycle: Make three holes near the edge of the card
Hang from hole 1 on a pin; hang a plumb line
Draw the vertical line along the string
Repeat with holes 2 and 3; lines cross at the centre of gravity

teach.heading: A beam with its own weight
bullets: A uniform beam's weight acts at its centre
Take moments about the pivot
Include the weight of the beam as a force
teach.note: Draw the ruler, label the pivot at 30 cm and the centre of gravity at 50 cm. Ask: which side does the beam's weight turn it? The upward force at the pivot has no moment about the pivot.

model.problem: A uniform metre rule weighs 1.2 N and is pivoted at the 30 cm mark. A weight hangs at the 5 cm mark to balance it. Find the weight.
steps: Rule's weight acts at 50 cm: distance from pivot = 20 cm = 0.20 m
Hung weight is at 25 cm = 0.25 m from the pivot

teach.heading: Stability
bullets: Stable: low centre of gravity and wide base
Tips when the weight line falls outside the base
Check: choose the correct reason
teach.note: Link to double-decker buses, which are tilt-tested, and racing cars. Ask pupils to tilt a box with a heavy base versus heavy top. Check using the options on the slide.

check.q: Why is a racing car with a low centre of gravity and wide wheelbase more stable?
options: The weight line stays inside the base until a larger tilt
check.why: The car can tilt further before the weight acts outside its base. Weight, momentum and drag are not the reason.

practice: A 25 N force acts 0.60 m from a pivot. Calculate the moment.
A 500 N boy sits 1.5 m from the pivot of a seesaw. Where must a 300 N girl sit to balance it?
Describe how to find the centre of gravity of an irregular piece of card.
independent: Core: A 40 N weight hangs 0.30 m left of a pivot. What force at 0.20 m on the right balances it?
Extend: A uniform 2.0 m plank weighs 80 N, pivoted at its centre. A 400 N person stands 0.50 m from one end. Where must a 600 N person stand to balance it?

Stretch: A 1.0 m uniform beam weighs 6.0 N and is pivoted at 0.20 m from one end. A 10 N weight hangs at the short end. Calculate the force needed 0.80 m from the pivot on the other side to keep it level, then the reaction force at the pivot.
exit: State the principle of moments.
A 50 N force acts 0.40 m from a pivot. Calculate the moment and give the unit.
lessons.homework: Write a method to find the centre of gravity of a lamina, listing the equipment and one safety precaution. Then complete four principle-of-moments problems.
lessons.send: SEND: give a labelled seesaw template: anticlockwise column and clockwise column. EAL: pre-teach pivot, clockwise, perpendicular. Stretch: include the pivot reaction force in the equilibrium of forces.
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Biology 4BI1, Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1; Science (Double Award) 4SD0

lessons.title: Mains electricity and safety: a.c., d.c., fuses and earthing
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a three-pin plug protect us when something goes wrong inside an appliance?
objectives: Compare a.c. and d.c.
Describe the live, neutral and earth wires of a plug
Explain how fuses, earthing, circuit breakers and insulation keep people safe
successCriteria: All: name the wires and their colours
Most: explain what a fuse and an earth wire do
Some: explain a fault sequence in a metal-cased appliance
lessons.crossCurricular: DT: product safety; Citizenship: electrical safety regulations
lessons.smsc: Moral: protecting life and property through care and responsibility

keywords.def: current that repeatedly reverses direction, as in UK mains (50 Hz)
current that flows in one direction only
a thin wire that melts if the current is too large, breaking the circuit
a safety wire that carries fault current safely to the ground

starter: Bismillah. State the SI unit of current and of potential difference.
Name the particles that carry current in a metal wire.
State the equation linking charge, current and time.

teach.heading: a.c. and d.c.
bullets: d.c.: flows one way (cells and batteries)
a.c.: reverses direction repeatedly
UK mains: about 230 V a.c., frequency 50 Hz
On an oscilloscope: d.c. is a flat line, a.c. is a wave
teach.note: Sketch both traces. Explain frequency 50 Hz means 50 complete reversals per second, so the period is 0.02 s. Ask pupils which type is used in their phone and which at the wall socket.

left.title: d.c.
points: Flat line on a voltage-time trace

teach.heading: Inside a three-pin plug
bullets: Live (brown): carries the supply voltage
Neutral (blue): completes the circuit
Earth (green and yellow): safety connection to the case
Fuse in the live wire
teach.note: Use a real plug or a labelled diagram. Ask why the fuse must be in the live wire: when it blows, the appliance is cut off from the 230 V. If it were in the neutral, the appliance would remain live. Switches also go in the live wire.

head: Part
Job
rows: melts when current is too high
stops the wires being pulled loose

teach.heading: What happens in a fault
bullets: A loose live wire touches the metal case
Case becomes live: a shock risk
Earth wire gives a low-resistance path to earth
Large current flows, fuse melts, appliance is isolated
teach.note: Walk through the steps slowly, and make clear that the earth wire only carries current when there is a fault. Mention circuit breakers (trip quickly, can be reset) and double-insulated appliances (plastic case, no earth wire needed).

model.problem: A toaster has a metal case. The live wire comes loose and touches the case. Explain how the earth wire and fuse protect the user.
steps: The earth wire connects the case to the ground
The live wire touching the case causes a large current through the earth wire
The large current heats and melts the fuse
The fuse breaks the live connection so the case is no longer live
model.answer: The fuse blows and isolates the toaster, so the case cannot give a shock

teach.heading: Danger zones
bullets: Damp conditions lower the body's resistance
Frayed cables expose live wires
Overloaded sockets can overheat
Wrong fuse rating is dangerous
teach.note: Stress practical safety: never use a plug with a damaged cable; never touch switches with wet hands; a fuse of too high a rating will not blow when it should. Discuss why protecting others from harm is part of good character.

misconception.wrong: The earth wire carries the current to make the appliance work.
misconception.right: The live and neutral wires carry the working current. The earth wire carries current only in a fault.

teach.heading: Check: where does the fuse go?
bullets: Select your answer
teach.note: Distractor B is a common error. Ask pupils to justify with a fault sequence.

check.q: In a three-pin plug the fuse is placed in the...
check.why: A fuse in the live wire disconnects the appliance from the 230 V supply when it blows. In the neutral wire, the appliance would stay connected to the live supply.

practice: State two differences between a.c. and d.c.
A plastic-cased hairdryer has no earth wire. Explain why it is still safe.
Explain why a fuse is placed in the live wire and not the neutral wire.
independent: Core: Label a diagram of a three-pin plug with wire colours and the fuse.
Extend: Explain why a person with wet hands is at greater risk of an electric shock.
Stretch: An a.c. supply has a period of 0.020 s. Calculate its frequency and say what happens to the direction of the current in 0.020 s.
exit: Name the three wires in a UK plug and their colours.
Explain what happens to an earthed metal appliance if the live wire touches the case.
lessons.homework: Make an electrical-safety poster for the home that includes three hazards and how a fuse, earth or circuit breaker protects against them.
lessons.send: SEND: colour-coded wire matching card and plug diagram. EAL: pre-teach live, neutral, fuse, earth. Stretch: explain residual current devices that compare live and neutral currents.
