lessons.title: Salt practicals: hydrated copper(II) sulfate and lead(II) sulfate
lessons.bigQuestion: How do you make a pure blue crystal from a black powder, and a white solid from two clear liquids?
objectives: Describe how to prepare pure, dry hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals from copper(II) oxide
Describe how to prepare pure, dry lead(II) sulfate by precipitation
Calculate theoretical and percentage yields
successCriteria: All: put the steps of each preparation in order
Most: explain the reason for each step, including using excess solid
Some: calculate the theoretical yield and evaluate losses
lessons.crossCurricular: Industry: making pigments and fertilisers; Maths: moles
lessons.smsc: Moral: safe handling of toxic lead compounds

keywords.def: more than is needed to react with all of the other reagent
a solution that can dissolve no more solute at that temperature
water chemically bound in crystals
reaction forming an insoluble solid from solutions

starter: Bismillah. State the solubility rule for sulfates.
Write the formula of copper(II) oxide.
Define a base.

teach.heading: Soluble salt: copper(II) sulfate
bullets: Warm dilute sulfuric acid in a beaker
Add black copper(II) oxide in small portions until it is in excess
Filter off the excess oxide
Heat filtrate to saturation, cool, filter, dry crystals
teach.note: Equation: CuO + H2SO4 gives CuSO4 + H2O. Excess copper(II) oxide ensures all the acid is used so the product is not contaminated by acid. The solution goes blue. Crystals are CuSO4.5H2O. Do not evaporate to dryness as that drives off the water of crystallisation. Dry crystals between filter papers.
cycle: Add CuO until no more dissolves (excess)
Heat the filtrate to the point of crystallisation
Cool, filter and dry the blue crystals

teach.heading: Insoluble salt: lead(II) sulfate
bullets: Mix lead(II) nitrate solution with dilute sulfuric acid
A white precipitate of lead(II) sulfate forms
Filter, wash with distilled water
Dry in a warm oven or between filter paper
teach.note: Equation: Pb(NO3)2(aq) + H2SO4(aq) gives PbSO4(s) + 2HNO3(aq). Sodium sulfate solution can also be used. Wash with distilled water to remove soluble nitrate impurities. Safety: lead compounds are toxic, so wear gloves, do not allow contact with skin or mouth, and wash hands. This is a Paper 2 only point (4CH1 separate Chemistry content, not Double Award).

teach.heading: Worked yield calculation
bullets: Moles of CuO = mass / Mr
1 mol CuO gives 1 mol hydrated crystals
Mass = moles x Mr of CuSO4.5H2O
Percentage yield = actual / theoretical x 100
teach.note: Use Ar: Cu 64, O 16, S 32, H 1 (Edexcel papers often use Cu = 63.5; follow the data given). Mr CuO = 80; Mr CuSO4.5H2O = 64 + 32 + 64 + 90 = 250.

model.problem: 4.0 g of copper(II) oxide forms CuSO4.5H2O. Mr of CuO = 80 and of CuSO4.5H2O = 250. Calculate the theoretical mass and the percentage yield if 9.5 g of crystals are collected.

teach.heading: Check: why excess?
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Option B is the trap: excess oxide would not make crystals grow faster. Pupils should link excess to complete reaction of the acid.

check.q: Why is excess copper(II) oxide added to warm sulfuric acid?
options: to ensure all the acid has reacted
check.why: Excess oxide makes sure no acid is left, and the leftover insoluble solid is removed by filtration.

teach.heading: Evaluating the practical
bullets: Why 76% not 100%?
Crystals left in solution or on filter paper
Not all dried completely
Handling losses
teach.note: Ask for two ways to improve the yield: cool slowly, wash with minimum cold water, avoid spillage.

practice: State why the filtrate is not heated until dry.
Write the equation for lead(II) nitrate reacting with sulfuric acid.
State a safety precaution when handling lead compounds.
independent: Core: Write a numbered method for preparing copper(II) sulfate crystals with a reason for each step.
Extend: Calculate the percentage yield for 2.0 g CuO giving 5.8 g of crystals (Mr CuO 80; CuSO4.5H2O 250).
Stretch: Compare the methods for copper(II) sulfate and lead(II) sulfate and explain why they differ.
exit: Name the solid removed by filtration in the copper(II) sulfate preparation.
Explain why lead(II) sulfate can be made by precipitation.
Big question: describe how to make each salt.
lessons.homework: Draw a flow chart for one preparation and annotate it with a reason for each step.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use a sequencing card sort. Stretch: explain why the precipitate is washed and what is in the washings.

lessons.title: Units of motion, v squared = u squared + 2as, and measuring motion
lessons.bigQuestion: How fast is a car going at the end of a ramp if we only know how far it travelled and how quickly it sped up?
objectives: Use the correct units for mass, distance, speed, acceleration, force, time and field strength
Use v2 = u2 + 2as to solve problems
Describe an experiment to investigate the motion of an everyday object
successCriteria: All: state the unit for each quantity
Most: use v2 = u2 + 2as with correct units
Some: plan and evaluate a practical to measure speed or acceleration of a toy car or ball
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: rearranging formulae; Sport: sprint starts
lessons.smsc: Social: precision and honest measurement

keywords.def: change in velocity per second, in m/s2
velocity at the start
velocity at the end
force per unit mass, in N/kg

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the average speed of a car that travels 150 m in 12 s.
State the equation linking force, mass and acceleration.
Describe what the gradient of a velocity-time graph shows.

teach.heading: Units you must know
bullets: Mass: kg; distance: m; time: s
Speed and velocity: m/s
Acceleration: m/s2; force: N
Gravitational field strength: N/kg
teach.note: Quick-fire: show a quantity, pupils show the unit. Link N/kg to weight: W = mg, so g is the weight of 1 kg: about 9.8 N/kg on Earth (use the value given in the question; 10 N/kg is often used, verify in the paper). Stress using base units in calculations: convert km/h or g or cm first.

teach.heading: The equation v2 = u2 + 2as
bullets: Use for constant acceleration in a straight line
v final velocity, u initial velocity, a acceleration, s distance
Needs no time
Take the square root at the end
teach.note: This equation comes from combining v = u + at and the average velocity rule. It is useful when time is not given. For a vehicle starting from rest u = 0. Remind pupils to square the speeds and not to forget the square root at the end.

model.problem: A toy car starts from rest and accelerates at 2.5 m/s2 over 20 m. Calculate its final velocity.

teach.heading: Check: stopping
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Option B forgot the square root. Option C is the common error of not squaring u. Ask which line of working each wrong answer came from.

check.q: A car at 20 m/s brakes with a deceleration of 5.0 m/s2 (a = -5.0). Which distance does it take to stop?
check.why: 0 = 20 squared + 2 x (-5) x s, so 400 = 10s and s = 40 m. 400 m is the value of u squared without dividing; 80 m comes from doubling the answer.

teach.heading: Practical: motion of everyday objects
bullets: Toy car down a ramp, or a tennis ball dropped
Measure distance with a metre rule
Time with a stopwatch or light gates
Repeat and find a mean; calculate speed or acceleration
teach.note: Plan: independent variable (ramp height or release height), dependent variable (time or speed), controlled variables (same car, same surface, same start position). Reaction time (about 0.2 s, approx.) is a significant error with a stopwatch over short times, so use a longer distance or light gates. Pupils calculate speed = distance / time; with velocity from rest, a = v / t. Safety: do not drop balls where people walk.
cycle: Mark start and finish at a measured distance
Release the object without pushing it
Time it from start to finish; repeat three times

teach.heading: Link the two
bullets: Time at start and end gives average speed
Light gates give speeds at two points
Then a = (v squared - u squared) / 2s
Compare with a prediction
teach.note: Suggest that pupils with light-gate data on a ramp can calculate acceleration from v2 = u2 + 2as. Discuss why friction makes the real value lower than predictions.

practice: State the unit of acceleration and of gravitational field strength.
A cyclist from rest accelerates at 1.5 m/s2 over 12 m. Calculate the final velocity.
Explain why a stopwatch is less accurate over a short fall.
independent: Core: Calculate final velocity for three sets of u, a and s.
Extend: A car travelling at 12 m/s accelerates at 2.0 m/s2 over 40 m. Calculate v.
Stretch: Design an experiment with a ramp to find the acceleration of a toy car and say how to reduce error.
exit: Calculate v for u = 0, a = 4.0 m/s2, s = 18 m.
State the unit of force and of mass.
Big question: what data do you need to find a car's final speed?
lessons.homework: Measure how long a ball takes to roll along a corridor three times and calculate the mean speed.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a triangle of symbols with units and a step-by-step template. Stretch: derive v2 = u2 + 2as from v = u + at and s = (u + v)t/2.

lessons.title: Extension and force: the practical, and where Hooke's law applies
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a spring return to its shape but a stretched rubber band does not follow the same rule?
objectives: Describe an experiment to measure extension against force for a spring, wire or rubber band
Plot and interpret a force-extension graph
Relate the initial straight section of the graph to Hooke's law
successCriteria: All: measure extension as new length minus original length
Most: identify the linear region and calculate the spring constant
Some: compare springs, wires and rubber bands and explain the limit of proportionality
lessons.crossCurricular: Engineering: suspension and safety harnesses; Maths: gradients
lessons.smsc: Social: trustworthy measurement and safe equipment

keywords.def: increase in length compared with the original length
force per unit extension, in N/m
point beyond which extension is no longer proportional to force
extension is directly proportional to force up to the limit of proportionality

starter: Bismillah. State the equation for weight.
Define elastic deformation.
Calculate the force needed to accelerate a 3 kg trolley at 2 m/s2.

teach.heading: Practical: extension against force
bullets: Clamp the spring and measure its original length
Add 1 N (100 g) masses in steps
Measure the new length each time
Extension = new length - original length
teach.note: Use a metre rule beside the spring; read at eye level to avoid parallax. Place a pointer or marker at the bottom of the spring. Safety: eye protection, a cushion or tray under the masses, and clamp stands should be stable. Repeat by unloading to check whether the spring returns to its original length. For wires use a long thin wire (such as steel) and small extensions; do not stretch wires to breaking point without protection.
cycle: Measure original length with no load
Add a mass and measure the length

teach.heading: The force-extension graph
bullets: Straight line through the origin at first
Gradient = spring constant k
Beyond the limit of proportionality the line curves
Beyond the elastic limit the spring may not return to shape
teach.note: Hooke's law: F = kx where F is force in N, x is extension in m and k is in N/m. Note: the limit of proportionality and the elastic limit are usually close; for a spring they are nearly the same point. For a rubber band the graph is not a straight line and it does not obey Hooke's law, while a metal wire obeys it for small loads only.

teach.heading: Worked example: spring constant
bullets: Use the straight part only
k = F / x
Convert cm to m before dividing
Units: N/m
teach.note: Stress: take values from the linear region, and ensure that x is in metres.

model.problem: A spring extends by 8.0 cm when a force of 4.0 N is applied in its linear region. Calculate the spring constant.

teach.heading: Check: reading the graph
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Option A is the trap: pupils often read off any point of the curve. Option C confuses the gradient with its reciprocal.

check.q: A force-extension graph is straight to 6 N then curves. What does the 6 N point show?
check.why: Beyond 6 N the extension is no longer proportional to force, so this is the limit of proportionality.

teach.heading: Evaluating the results
bullets: Parallax and ruler resolution cause errors
Spring may be damaged if overloaded
Repeat loading and unloading
Plot the line of best fit
teach.note: Discuss: why not add loads until the spring breaks? Include safety and reliability. A line of best fit should pass through the origin in the linear region.

practice: A spring has k = 25 N/m. Calculate the force for an extension of 0.20 m.
State what 'limit of proportionality' means.
Describe how to measure extension accurately.
independent: Core: Plot the data given by your teacher and draw a line of best fit through the linear region.
Extend: Calculate k from the gradient and state the unit.
Stretch: Explain the differences between graphs for a spring, a wire and a rubber band.
exit: Calculate F for k = 40 N/m and x = 0.15 m.
Name two sources of error in the practical.
Big question: where does Hooke's law stop working?
lessons.homework: Find a spring-based object at home (pen spring, door stop) and describe how you would test whether it follows Hooke's law.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a pre-drawn axis and a sentence frame for the limit of proportionality. Stretch: calculate the energy stored in a spring (beyond the specification; verify).

lessons.title: Forces on a beam: how supports share the load
lessons.bigQuestion: Two people carry a heavy box on a plank. Who feels the larger force and why?
objectives: Describe how the upward forces on a light beam change with the position of a heavy object
Calculate the support forces using moments
Describe an experiment to investigate them
successCriteria: All: say which support carries more load when the object is closer to it
Most: calculate both support forces for a simple beam
Some: explain results using the principle of moments and equilibrium
lessons.crossCurricular: Engineering: bridges and shelves; Design technology
lessons.smsc: Social: shared responsibility, like sharing a load fairly

keywords.def: force x perpendicular distance from the pivot, in N m
state with no resultant force and no resultant moment
beam whose weight is small enough to ignore
upward force from a support

starter: Bismillah. State the equation for the moment of a force.
State two conditions for a body to be in equilibrium.
Calculate the moment of a 20 N force 0.30 m from a pivot.

teach.heading: The setup
bullets: A light beam rests on two supports
A heavy object sits on the beam
Each support pushes upward
Beam is in equilibrium
teach.note: Paper 2 only: this point is separate Physics (4PH1) content, not in Double Award. Draw the beam with a load W at distance x from the left support, supports at each end separated by L. Treat the beam weight as negligible (a light beam). Ask: if the load is over the left support, how much does the right support carry? (Almost nothing.)

quote.text: Upward forces on the supports always add up to the weight of the load (plus the beam's weight if it is not negligible).

teach.heading: What changes as the load moves
bullets: Load closer to a support: that support carries more
Load in the middle: equal forces
Sum of the two upward forces stays constant
Use moments about one support to calculate
teach.note: Take moments about the left support: clockwise moment of the load = W x x. Anticlockwise moment of the right support = R(right) x L. So R(right) = W x / L. Then R(left) = W - R(right). The principle of moments says total clockwise moments equal total anticlockwise moments for a body in equilibrium.

teach.heading: Worked example
bullets: Take moments about the left support
Clockwise = anticlockwise
Find the right support force
Subtract to find the left force
teach.note: Check the sum equals the load as a final step.

model.problem: A light beam 1.0 m long rests on supports at each end. A 12 N weight is placed 0.25 m from the left end. Calculate both support forces.
steps: Moments about left end: 12 x 0.25 = R(right) x 1.0

teach.heading: Check: the beam
bullets: Hinge question
teach.note: Option B is the mistaken idea that supports always share equally. D mixes up which side is bigger.

check.q: A heavy load sits closer to the right support of a light beam. Which statement is true?
options: the right support carries a bigger force
the left support carries a bigger force
check.why: Taking moments about the left support shows the right support must carry more when the load is nearer to it.

teach.heading: Practical idea
bullets: Metre rule on two newton meters
Place a 5 N weight at different points
Record both readings
The sum should equal the weight
teach.note: Online option: demonstrate and let pupils record readings from video. Safety: use a small weight and keep feet away. If the ruler is not light, include its weight at the 50 cm mark; discuss as a source of error.

practice: A light beam is 2.0 m long. A 30 N load is 0.50 m from the left support. Calculate the right support force.
State what happens to both support forces as the load moves to the middle.
Explain why the sum of support forces equals the load.
independent: Core: Complete a table of left and right forces for loads at 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 m on a 1.0 m beam carrying 10 N.
Extend: Draw a graph of right-hand force against load position and describe it.
Stretch: Include the weight of a uniform 4.0 N beam (weight acts at the midpoint) and recalculate.
exit: Which support carries the bigger force when the load is nearer to it?
Calculate R(right) for a 20 N load 0.40 m from left on a 1.0 m light beam.
Big question: who carries more on the plank?
lessons.homework: Describe a real structure (bridge, shelf or seesaw) and explain how loads are shared between supports.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a labelled beam diagram and equation steps. Stretch: use two unknown positions and solve for the load position.

lessons.title: Electrical units, charge Q = It and two resistors in series
lessons.bigQuestion: How much charge passes through a torch bulb in a minute, and how do two resistors share the voltage?
objectives: State the units A, C, J, ohm, s, V and W
Use Q = It
Calculate the current, voltage and resistance for two resistors in series
successCriteria: All: state the unit for each electrical quantity
Most: use Q = It and V = IR with correct units
Some: solve multi-step series circuit problems including charge
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: rearranging; Engineering: circuit design
lessons.smsc: Social: safe and careful use of electricity

keywords.def: property of particles that makes them feel electrical force, measured in coulombs
rate of flow of charge, in amperes
energy transferred per unit charge, in volts
opposition to current, in ohms

starter: Bismillah. State the equation linking potential difference, current and resistance.
Name the instrument that measures current and say how it is connected.
Calculate the current when 12 V is applied to a 4 ohm resistor.

teach.heading: Units to know
bullets: Current: ampere (A); charge: coulomb (C)
Potential difference: volt (V)
Resistance: ohm; energy: joule (J)
Power: watt (W); time: second (s)
teach.note: Quick-fire quiz of quantity to unit. Link: 1 A = 1 °C/s; 1 V = 1 J/C; 1 W = 1 J/s. Common slip: confusing coulomb (charge) with the ampere (current) and writing ohm as 'o'. The ohm symbol is the Greek capital omega.

teach.heading: Charge = current x time
bullets: Q = I t
Q in coulombs, I in amperes, t in seconds
Convert minutes to seconds
One coulomb is one ampere for one second
teach.note: Ask pupils to say it in words: current is the charge passing each second. Always convert time to seconds first.

model.problem: A current of 0.50 A flows through a lamp for 2.0 minutes. Calculate the charge that passes.
steps: I = 0.50 A and t = 2.0 minutes = 120 s

teach.heading: Resistors in series
bullets: Same current through each resistor
Voltages across resistors add up to the supply
Total resistance R = R1 + R2
Current = supply voltage / total resistance
teach.note: Draw a 6.0 V cell with a 4.0 ohm and an 8.0 ohm resistor in series. Total R = 12 ohm. I = 6.0/12 = 0.50 A. The bigger resistor gets the bigger share of voltage: V1 = 0.50 x 4.0 = 2.0 V, V2 = 0.50 x 8.0 = 4.0 V. Check 2.0 + 4.0 = 6.0 V.

model.problem: A 6.0 V cell supplies a 4.0 ohm and an 8.0 ohm resistor in series. Calculate the current and the voltage across each resistor.
model.answer: 0.50 A; 2.0 V and 4.0 V (which add to 6.0 V)

teach.heading: Check: series circuit
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Option B adds the currents, the usual parallel mistake. Option D treats the current as splitting.

check.q: Two resistors are in series with a 9 V supply. The current in the first is 0.3 A. What is the current in the second?
check.why: In a series circuit the same current flows through every component.

teach.heading: Putting it together
bullets: Find total resistance first
Then the current
Then each voltage
Check voltages add to the supply
teach.note: Do a mixed worked problem with charge: how much charge passes through the circuit in 2 minutes with I = 0.50 A? Q = 0.50 x 120 = 60 °C. Emphasise unit checks at each line.

practice: State the unit of charge and of power.
Calculate the charge when 3.0 A flows for 5.0 s.
Two resistors of 5.0 ohm and 10 ohm are in series with a 9.0 V supply. Calculate the current.
independent: Core: Calculate Q for three combinations of I and t, converting time units.
Extend: For a 12 V supply with resistors 10 ohm and 20 ohm in series find the current and the voltage across each.
Stretch: A series circuit has a 12 V supply, current 0.40 A and one resistor of 10 ohm. Calculate the second resistance and the charge in 5 minutes.
exit: State two units that equal J/C and C/s.
Calculate the charge for 0.20 A over 30 s.
Big question: how do resistors share the voltage?
lessons.homework: Draw a series circuit and calculate current and voltage across each of two resistors of your choice.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a formula table with units and a template layout for each calculation. Stretch: explain why bulbs in series are dimmer.

lessons.title: The heating effect of a current, a.c. and d.c., and indicator lamps
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a toaster glow while its cable stays cool, and why does a phone charger not run on the mains directly?
objectives: Explain how a current in a resistor transfers energy and raises its temperature
Distinguish alternating current from direct current
Describe how lamps and LEDs show a current is flowing
successCriteria: All: name three appliances using the heating effect
Most: explain the heating effect using collisions between electrons and ions and calculate energy
Some: compare a.c. and d.c. and explain why LEDs need protection
lessons.crossCurricular: Engineering: heating elements; Design technology
lessons.smsc: Moral: avoiding waste of energy (israf)

keywords.def: energy transferred to thermal energy when a current flows through a resistor
current that repeatedly changes direction
current that flows in one direction only
light-emitting diode, which lights when a current flows in the correct direction

starter: Bismillah. State the equation for electrical power.
Calculate the power when 230 V drives a current of 5.0 A.
Name the safety device that melts if the current is too high.

teach.heading: Why wires heat up
bullets: Electrons collide with ions in the metal
Ions vibrate more, so the temperature rises
Electrical energy transfers to thermal energy
More resistance: more heating
teach.note: Link to particle model: moving electrons transfer energy to the lattice ions. Heating elements (kettles, toasters, electric fires, immersion heaters) are made of high resistance wire, often an alloy such as nichrome, which stays hot without melting. The supply cables are made of low resistance copper so they stay cooler. Energy transferred: E = I V t = P t.

teach.heading: Worked example: kettle energy
bullets: E = P t
Power in watts, time in seconds
Convert kW to W and minutes to s
Energy in joules
teach.note: Mention that kWh is another unit on bills but joules are the SI unit.

model.problem: A kettle rated 2.3 kW is switched on for 3.0 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred.
model.answer: 414 000 J (about 4.1 x 10 to the power 5 J)

teach.heading: Alternating and direct current
bullets: Cells and batteries supply d.c.
UK mains is a.c.: 230 V and 50 Hz
a.c. changes direction 50 times per second (cycles)
Oscilloscope trace: d.c. is flat; a.c. is a wave
teach.note: The mains in the UK is about 230 V at 50 Hz (verify with the board's data sheet). Draw an oscilloscope trace of each: d.c. is a horizontal line, a.c. is a sine wave about zero. Chargers and adaptors convert a.c. to d.c. A cell has a fixed positive and negative terminal, so the current is always in one direction.

teach.heading: Check: a.c. or d.c.?
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Option B reverses the cell. Option C is the typical confusion that a.c. goes in only one direction.

check.q: Which statement about the supply is correct?
options: a.c. flows in one direction only
d.c. changes direction 50 times per second
check.why: The mains supply is alternating current. Batteries supply direct current.

teach.heading: Lamps and LEDs as indicators
bullets: A lit lamp or LED shows a current flows
LED needs a resistor to limit the current
LED lights only one way round
Use in standby lights and chargers
teach.note: Ask: if the LED is not lit, does that mean no current anywhere? (It may be reversed or the circuit is broken.) LEDs use less energy than filament lamps because less energy is wasted as heat. Do not connect an LED directly to a cell without a series resistor as it could burn out.

practice: Explain why the heating element of a toaster has high resistance.
State the frequency of UK mains.
Calculate the energy transferred when a 1.5 kW heater is on for 20 s.
independent: Core: List four appliances using the heating effect and say what the element heats.
Extend: Explain why electric cables are made of copper while heater elements are not.
Stretch: Calculate the energy in joules and in kWh for a 2.0 kW heater on for 30 minutes (1 kWh = 3 600 000 J).
exit: State the energy transfer in a heating element.
Name a source of d.c.
Big question: why does the toaster glow while the cable does not?
lessons.homework: Look at the label on a mains appliance and record its power and voltage. Calculate its current using P = IV.

lessons.title: Why homes use parallel circuits, and how resistance changes the current
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does one broken bulb at home not put all the lights out?
objectives: Explain why parallel circuits are used for domestic lighting and series circuits for other uses
Describe qualitatively how changing resistance affects the current
Calculate current for different resistances at a fixed voltage
successCriteria: All: compare what happens in series and parallel when a bulb breaks
Most: explain how a variable resistor changes brightness
Some: predict changes in current when resistors are added in series or in parallel
lessons.crossCurricular: Design technology: lighting; Engineering
lessons.smsc: Social: consideration of others when sharing resources

keywords.def: components in one loop, so there is only one path
components on separate branches, so there is more than one path
a resistor whose resistance can be changed by hand
one path in a parallel circuit

starter: Bismillah. State the equation linking V, I and R.
Calculate the total resistance of 3.0 ohm and 5.0 ohm in series.
State what happens to the current at a junction.

teach.heading: Series versus parallel
bullets: Series: one path; all stop if one breaks
Series: voltage is shared between components
Parallel: each branch has the full supply voltage
Parallel: other branches work if one breaks
teach.note: Use a Christmas-lights example: older series sets went out entirely when one bulb failed. Mains lighting uses parallel branches so each lamp has 230 V, can be switched independently, and has full brightness. Series is useful when you want a component to work only if all conditions are met (e.g. a safety interlock where all switches must be closed).

teach.heading: Resistance and current
bullets: At a fixed voltage, more resistance means less current
I = V / R
A variable resistor dims or brightens a lamp
A thermistor or LDR changes resistance with conditions
teach.note: Link the qualitative idea to the formula: double the resistance and the current halves for a fixed voltage. A variable resistor in series with a lamp: increasing its resistance reduces current, dimming the lamp. Adding resistors in series increases total resistance and lowers current; adding in parallel provides extra paths so total resistance falls and the supply current rises.

model.problem: A 12 V supply is connected to a 6.0 ohm resistor and then to a 12 ohm resistor. Calculate the current each time and describe the pattern.
steps: Doubling the resistance halved the current
model.answer: 2.0 A then 1.0 A: more resistance, less current.

teach.heading: Check: parallel branches
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Option B comes from thinking the cell voltage is shared in parallel. D confuses current with voltage.

check.q: Three identical lamps are connected in parallel to a 6 V cell. What is the voltage across each lamp?
check.why: Each branch of a parallel circuit has the full cell voltage, so 6 V.

teach.heading: Why does the supply current rise?
bullets: More branches give more paths
Total resistance of parallel branches falls
Supply current is the sum of the branch currents
So too many appliances on one socket is dangerous
teach.note: Ask: what happens if many appliances are plugged into one extension lead? The currents add, so the cable overheats, which is why fuses are used and why we avoid overloading sockets. Link to earlier mains safety lessons.

practice: Explain why lamps in a house are in parallel.
A 9.0 V supply is connected to a 18 ohm resistor. Calculate the current.
State what happens to the current if the resistance of a variable resistor is increased.
independent: Core: Draw a series and a parallel circuit for two lamps and state one advantage of each.
Extend: Explain what happens to the other lamps if one lamp breaks in each circuit.
Stretch: Explain why adding another branch increases the current drawn from the supply.
exit: State one reason domestic lamps are in parallel.
Calculate I for 12 V and 24 ohm.
Big question: why does one broken bulb not put all the lights out?
lessons.homework: Draw the lighting circuit for two rooms with a switch for each and explain why it is wired in parallel.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give circuit pictures to label with series or parallel. Stretch: calculate the current for two 12 ohm resistors in parallel on a 12 V supply (2.0 A in total).

lessons.title: Static electricity: conductors, insulators, attraction, dangers and uses
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a charged balloon stick to a wall, and how can static electricity cause a fire or print a page?
objectives: Identify common conductors and insulators
Explain attraction and repulsion between charged objects
Describe dangers of static electricity when fuelling and uses in photocopiers and inkjet printers
successCriteria: All: sort materials into conductors and insulators and state the rule for charges
Most: explain charging by friction with electron transfer
Some: explain a danger and a use in detail, including precautions
lessons.crossCurricular: Engineering: fuel safety; Technology: printing
lessons.smsc: Moral: safety and care for others when handling fuel

keywords.def: material that does not allow charge to flow easily
material that allows charge to flow easily
movement of electrons from one object to another when charged
connecting an object to the ground so charge flows away

starter: Bismillah. Name the particle that moves when objects become charged by friction.
State what charge a proton and an electron carry.
Define electric current.

teach.heading: Conductors and insulators
bullets: Metals are conductors
Plastics, glass, rubber and dry air are insulators
Insulators can hold a static charge
Conductors let charge flow away
teach.note: Paper 2 only: this section is separate Physics (4PH1) content, not in Double Award. Do a quick sort of materials. Plastic handles on electrical equipment protect users; metals in cables carry current. Ask why a metal rod held in the hand does not stay charged (the charge flows through you to the ground) while a plastic rod does.

teach.heading: Charging and the force between charges
bullets: Rubbing transfers electrons from one material to another
The material gaining electrons becomes negative
Like charges repel; unlike charges attract
Charged objects attract uncharged light objects
teach.note: Polythene rod rubbed with cloth: electrons move from the cloth to the rod, the rod becomes negative, the cloth positive. Only electrons move; protons stay fixed in the nucleus. A charged rod attracts small paper pieces because of induced charge: electrons in the paper are pushed away or pulled towards the rod, leaving the nearer end opposite to the rod.

model.problem: A polythene rod rubbed with a woollen cloth becomes negatively charged. Explain why, and say what the rod does to a second negative rod.
steps: Friction transfers electrons from the wool to the polythene
The polythene gains electrons so it is negative
The wool loses electrons so it is positive
Two negative rods are like charges, so they repel
model.answer: Electrons move to the rod; the two negative rods repel.

teach.heading: Check: charges
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Option B shows the common idea that positive charges move. Option D reverses the rule.

check.q: A balloon is rubbed on hair and becomes negative. Which statement is correct?
check.why: Only electrons move. The balloon gained electrons, so it is negative; the hair lost them.

teach.heading: Dangers: fuelling aircraft and tankers
bullets: Friction of fuel in pipes builds up charge
A spark can ignite fuel vapour
Earth the aircraft or tanker
Bond (connect) the vehicle and the hose
teach.note: Fuel flowing through hoses causes friction which separates charge. If the charge builds until a spark jumps, it can ignite fuel vapour, causing a fire or explosion. Precautions: earthing straps or wires, conductive hoses and connecting the tanker and aircraft with a conducting cable so they stay at the same potential so charge cannot build up. Lightning is another example to mention.
cycle: Electrons transfer and charge builds up
A spark can jump to a nearby conductor
Prevent this by earthing and bonding

teach.heading: Uses: photocopiers and inkjet printers
bullets: Photocopier: charged drum attracts toner powder
Light discharges the white areas
Toner transfers to paper and is heated
Inkjet: ink drops are charged and deflected by plates
teach.note: Photocopier: image of the page is projected on a charged drum; the light-struck areas lose charge; the remaining charged areas attract oppositely charged toner; toner is transferred to the paper and fixed by heat. Inkjet: tiny ink drops are given a charge and deflected by charged plates to the correct place on the paper. Ask pupils to identify the attraction and repulsion in each.

practice: State which materials are good insulators.
Explain why an aircraft is earthed when it is refuelled.
State one use of static electricity.
independent: Core: Sort ten materials into conductors and insulators and write the charge rule.
Extend: Explain how a photocopier uses static electricity in four steps.
Stretch: Explain why a metal fuel tanker is joined to the ground by a conductor but a plastic container can store a charge.
exit: State the rule for charges.
State one danger of static electricity in fuelling.
Big question: write one sentence for a danger and one for a use.
lessons.homework: Describe an everyday example of static electricity (for example a jumper) and explain it in terms of electrons.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide diagrams for each step. Stretch: explain why charged objects attract uncharged objects.

lessons.title: Measuring the speed of sound and linking loudness to amplitude
lessons.bigQuestion: How could you measure the speed of sound with just a wall, a clap and a stopwatch?
objectives: State the units degree, Hz, m, m/s and s
Describe an experiment to measure the speed of sound in air
Relate the loudness of a sound to the amplitude of the source's vibration
successCriteria: All: give the unit for each wave quantity
Most: calculate the speed of sound from distance and time
Some: evaluate the experiment and link amplitude to loudness and frequency to pitch
lessons.crossCurricular: Music: loudness and pitch; Engineering: sonar and ultrasound
lessons.smsc: Social: protecting hearing (a trust from Allah)

keywords.def: maximum displacement of a wave from its rest position
number of waves passing a point per second, in hertz
reflected sound
how loud a sound is; depends on amplitude

starter: Bismillah. State the wave equation.
Define frequency and give its unit.
State whether sound is transverse or longitudinal.

teach.heading: Wave units
bullets: Frequency: hertz (Hz)
Wavelength and distance: metre (m)
Speed: metre per second (m/s)
Time: second (s); angle: degree
teach.note: Quick-fire quiz. Remind: v = f x lambda and f = 1/T, with T in seconds. Angles in this unit are measured in degrees from the normal. Pupils should convert kHz to Hz and cm to m before substituting.

teach.heading: Practical: speed of sound
bullets: Method 1: echo from a distant wall
Measure the distance to the wall with a trundle wheel
Time between a clap and its echo
Speed = 2 x distance / time
teach.note: Paper 2 only: this practical is separate Physics (4PH1) content, not in Double Award. The sound travels to the wall and back, so the total distance is twice the distance to the wall. Alternative: two microphones a measured distance apart connected to a timer, or a starting-pistol method. Mention that the speed of sound in air is about 330-340 m/s, depending on temperature (approx.; verify). Repeat and take a mean; use a long distance to reduce the effect of reaction time.
cycle: Measure the distance d to a large wall
Stop it when the echo is heard
Repeat to find the mean time t

teach.heading: Worked example
bullets: Total distance is there and back
v = distance / time
Check the answer is about 340 m/s
teach.note: Pupils often forget to double the distance.

model.problem: A pupil stands 85 m from a wall. The echo is heard 0.50 s after the clap. Calculate the speed of sound.

teach.heading: Check: echo
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Option A forgets to double the distance. Option D inverts the formula.

check.q: A clap echoes from a wall 60 m away after 0.35 s. Which calculation gives the speed?
check.why: The sound travels 60 m to the wall and 60 m back, so the distance is 120 m. Speed = distance / time.

teach.heading: Loudness and amplitude
bullets: Louder sound: larger amplitude of vibration
Pitch is controlled by frequency
Higher frequency: higher pitch
Amplitude does not change the speed of sound
teach.note: Paper 2 only (3.29P, separate Physics 4PH1 content). Show an oscilloscope or phone app trace: a louder note has taller waves, a higher note has more waves in the same time. Common mistake: saying a louder sound has higher frequency. Louder sounds carry more energy.

misconception.wrong: A louder sound has a higher frequency.
misconception.right: Loudness depends on amplitude. A higher frequency gives a higher pitch, not a louder sound.

practice: Calculate the speed of a sound that travels 680 m in 2.0 s.
State what happens to the waveform on an oscilloscope when a sound gets louder.
Explain why the distance is doubled in the echo method.
independent: Core: Calculate the speed of sound for three sets of distance and time data.
Extend: A pupil stands 100 m from a wall and measures 0.60 s for the echo. Calculate the speed and comment on the accuracy.
Stretch: Suggest two improvements to the experiment and explain how each reduces error.
exit: State the unit of frequency.
Explain how amplitude relates to loudness.
Big question: describe how to measure the speed of sound.
lessons.homework: Use a phone tone-generator app to compare a high and low note, and describe what changes on a screen trace.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide wave sketches to label. Stretch: explain why sound travels faster in warmer air (approx.; verify).

lessons.title: The continuous electromagnetic spectrum: speed, hazards and protection
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is sunlight good for us in small amounts but dangerous in large amounts, and why does a mobile phone not cook us?
objectives: Describe the electromagnetic spectrum as continuous and travelling at the same speed in free space
Use v = f x lambda for electromagnetic waves
Describe the harmful effects of excess exposure to microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet and gamma rays and how to protect against them
successCriteria: All: order the spectrum and name a use and hazard
Most: calculate wavelength or frequency using the speed of light
Some: explain hazards in terms of energy absorbed by cells and justify protections
lessons.crossCurricular: Health: skin cancer prevention; Technology: communication
lessons.smsc: Moral: care for our own health and others' health

keywords.def: the continuous family of waves from radio to gamma rays
a vacuum with no matter
radiation with enough energy to damage cells by removing electrons from atoms
wave where oscillations are at right angles to the direction of travel

starter: Bismillah. List the seven regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing frequency.
State one use of radio waves.
State the wave equation.

teach.heading: One spectrum, one speed
bullets: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma
They merge continuously; the divisions are not sharp
All transverse and all travel at 3.0 x 10 to the power 8 m/s in free space
They differ in wavelength and frequency
teach.note: Light is just one small part of the spectrum. Increasing frequency: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma. Wavelength decreases as frequency increases because the speed is fixed. Quote the speed of light as 3.0 x 10 to the power 8 m/s (verify the value given in the data sheet). Ask: how do we know that radio waves and light are the same kind of wave? (Same speed in a vacuum.)
cycle: Gamma rays: shortest wavelength, highest frequency

teach.heading: Worked example: wavelength of radio
bullets: v = f x lambda
v = 3.0 x 10 to the power 8 m/s
Rearrange for lambda
lambda = v / f
teach.note: Convert MHz to Hz first: 1 MHz = 1 x 10 to the power 6 Hz.

model.problem: A radio station broadcasts at 100 MHz. Calculate the wavelength. (v = 3.0 x 10 to the power 8 m/s)
steps: f = 100 MHz = 1.0 x 10 to the power 8 Hz
lambda = 3.0 x 10 to the power 8 / 1.0 x 10 to the power 8

teach.heading: Check: spectrum facts
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Option A is a typical misconception that EM waves slow down as frequency rises. Option C confuses the order of frequency.

check.q: Which statement about all electromagnetic waves is correct?
options: they travel at different speeds in a vacuum
they travel at the same speed in a vacuum
they need a medium to travel
check.why: All EM waves travel at the same speed in free space (about 3.0 x 10 to the power 8 m/s) and are transverse.

teach.heading: Harmful effects and protection
bullets: Microwaves: heat body cells (internal heating)
Infrared: skin burns
Ultraviolet: sunburn, skin cancer, eye damage
Gamma: cell damage, mutations, cancer
teach.note: Higher-frequency waves such as ultraviolet and gamma carry more energy per photon and can ionise atoms, damaging DNA. Protection: sunscreen, clothing and sunglasses for UV; limit time and use thick lead or concrete shielding for gamma; keep microwave oven doors sealed (the metal mesh reflects microwaves); avoid touching hot objects and use sunscreen. Be careful with mobile phone claims: the evidence for health harm at normal exposure is not established; note 'verify' with a current health authority.

head: Radiation
Harm from excess
Protection
rows: lead or thick concrete, limit time

practice: List the regions of the spectrum from lowest to highest frequency.
Calculate the frequency of light with a wavelength of 6.0 x 10 to the power -7 m (v = 3.0 x 10 to the power 8 m/s).
State one protection against ultraviolet.
independent: Core: Complete a table of use, hazard and protection for four types of radiation.
Extend: Calculate the wavelength of a microwave of frequency 2.5 GHz (2.5 x 10 to the power 9 Hz).
Stretch: Explain why gamma rays are more dangerous than radio waves in terms of energy.
exit: State the speed of EM waves in a vacuum.
Name one danger of excess ultraviolet.
Big question: why is sunlight both good and harmful?
lessons.homework: Research the UV index and write advice for a family going to the beach.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use an ordered picture strip of the spectrum. Stretch: explain why UV is absorbed by the ozone layer.

lessons.title: Refraction practical and the refractive index n = sin i / sin r
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we measure how strongly glass bends light?
objectives: Describe an experiment with rectangular blocks, semicircular blocks and prisms to investigate refraction
Measure angles of incidence and refraction
Calculate the refractive index using n = sin i / sin r
successCriteria: All: draw the normal and label i and r
Most: calculate n from measured angles
Some: plot sin i against sin r and use the gradient to find n
lessons.crossCurricular: Optics: lenses and glasses; Maths: trigonometry
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflecting on light and the design of the eye

keywords.def: a line at right angles to the surface at the point where the ray meets it
angle between the incident ray and the normal
angle between the refracted ray and the normal
how much a material bends light: n = sin i / sin r

starter: Bismillah. State what happens to the speed of light as it enters glass from air.
State the direction a ray bends when entering a denser medium.
Calculate sin 30 degrees using a calculator in degree mode.

teach.heading: Practical: refraction in glass
bullets: Place a rectangular block on paper and trace it
Shine a ray at the block at several angles
Mark the entering and emerging rays
Draw the normal; measure i and r with a protractor
teach.note: Use a ray box with a single slit or a laser pointer (class 2 only; never shine into eyes). Pupils join the entering and emerging points inside the block to find the refracted ray. Angles are always measured from the normal, not the surface. For semicircular blocks, aim along the radius so the ray enters the curved face without bending. Prisms show dispersion for white light. Use a sharp pencil, measure to the nearest degree and repeat.
cycle: Mark the incident ray with two crosses
Mark the emerging ray with two crosses
Remove the block and join the points
Draw the normal and measure i and r

teach.heading: The refractive index
bullets: n = sin i / sin r
i in air, r in the material
n has no unit
For glass, n is about 1.5
teach.note: Ask pupils to check calculators are in degrees mode. A larger n means more bending. Water is about 1.33 and diamond about 2.4 (approx.). When light enters from air into the material, i is in air. Snell's law is the name used for this relationship. Typical measured values for glass lie between 1.4 and 1.6.

model.problem: A ray enters glass from air with i = 40 degrees and r = 25 degrees. Calculate the refractive index.

teach.heading: Check: the angles
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Option A measures from the surface rather than the normal. Option C is the trap of using angle only, forgetting the sine.

check.q: Which pair of angles should be used in n = sin i / sin r?
options: the angle between the incident and refracted ray
the angle of the block corner
check.why: Both angles are measured from the normal, not the surface.

teach.heading: Using a graph
bullets: Plot sin i (y) against sin r (x)
A straight line through the origin shows sin i is proportional to sin r
Gradient = refractive index
Reduces random error compared with one reading
teach.note: Collect 5 or 6 pairs of angles, calculate the sines and plot. The gradient equals n. A single-measurement n can be badly affected by a reading error, but a line of best fit uses all the data. Anomalies are easy to spot on a graph.

teach.heading: Block shapes
bullets: Rectangular block: emerging ray parallel to the incident ray
Semicircular block: ray along radius is undeviated at the curve
Prism: ray bends towards the base
White light disperses into a spectrum
teach.note: Ask: why does the emergent ray from the rectangular block run parallel to the incident ray? (Bends towards the normal on entry and by the same amount away on exit.) Prism sets up the link to dispersion: different colours have slightly different values of n.

practice: Calculate n if i = 50 degrees and r = 30 degrees.
State why the normal is drawn.
State what the gradient of a sin i against sin r graph represents.
independent: Core: Calculate n for three pairs of angles.
Extend: Plot sin i against sin r for six pairs of readings and find the gradient.
Stretch: Explain why the emerging ray from a rectangular block is parallel to the incident ray.
exit: Calculate n for i = 45 and r = 28 degrees.
State one safety rule with ray boxes.
Big question: how do we measure the bending power of glass?
lessons.homework: Use a clear glass of water and a pencil to observe refraction; sketch and explain what you see.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a protractor guide and a calculation template. Stretch: calculate n for water if i = 35 degrees and r = 25.5 degrees (approx. 1.35).
lessons.board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) Biology 4BI1, Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1; Science (Double Award) 4SD0

lessons.title: Finding the critical angle with a semicircular block
lessons.bigQuestion: At what angle does light stop leaving glass and start bouncing back inside?
objectives: Define the critical angle c
Describe an experiment to find the critical angle with a semicircular block
Use sin c = 1 / n to calculate the critical angle
successCriteria: All: state what happens to light at angles less than, equal to and greater than c
Most: use the semicircular block experiment to find c
Some: calculate c from n and explain why only denser to less dense boundaries have a critical angle
lessons.crossCurricular: Technology: optical fibres and endoscopes; Cycling: reflectors
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: appreciating the precision of natural laws

keywords.def: angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction is 90 degrees
all light reflected inside the denser medium when the angle exceeds c
a medium with higher refractive index
thin glass strand that carries light by repeated total internal reflection

starter: Bismillah. State the equation for refractive index.
Calculate n for i = 30 and r = 19.5 degrees.
State what happens to the speed of light when it moves from glass to air.

teach.heading: What is the critical angle?
bullets: Light goes from glass (dense) towards air
Small i: light mostly refracts out
At i = c: refracted ray runs along the surface
Beyond c: total internal reflection
teach.note: Draw three rays: i less than c, i equal to c (angle of refraction 90 degrees), i greater than c (total internal reflection). A weak reflected ray is also seen at small angles. Total internal reflection needs two conditions: the light is travelling in the denser medium and i is greater than c.

head: Angle of incidence
What happens
rows: most light refracts out, a little reflects
refracted ray travels along the boundary

teach.heading: Experiment: semicircular block
bullets: Place the block with the flat face on a protractor
Aim the ray at the centre of the flat face along a radius
Increase i slowly from the curved side
Note i when the emerging ray vanishes along the surface
teach.note: Because the ray enters along the radius it is not bent at the curved face, so the angle at the flat face equals the angle on the protractor. Find c as the angle at which the refracted ray just disappears along the flat face. Repeat three times and take a mean. Safety: ray box lamps get hot, so do not touch.
cycle: Aim the ray at the flat face's centre
Start with a small angle of incidence
Record the angle when the refracted ray skims the surface

teach.heading: Link to refractive index
bullets: At i = c, r = 90 degrees
n = sin 90 / sin c = 1 / sin c
So sin c = 1 / n
Higher n gives a smaller critical angle
teach.note: Using n = sin i/sin r in reverse: for light leaving the material the roles swap. At the critical angle sin r = sin 90 = 1, giving sin c = 1/n.

model.problem: Glass has a refractive index of 1.50. Calculate its critical angle.

teach.heading: Check: total internal reflection
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Option A is a typical error: TIR can't happen from air to glass. Option C confuses the critical angle with 90 degrees.

check.q: Light in glass hits the glass-air boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle. What happens?
options: it refracts out of the glass
it is totally reflected back into the glass
it speeds up in the glass
check.why: Above the critical angle there is no refracted ray, so all the light is totally internally reflected.

teach.heading: Where it is used
bullets: Optical fibres carry signals
Prisms in binoculars
Cat's-eye reflectors
Endoscopes in medicine
teach.note: Ask pupils to explain an optical fibre: light enters at a small angle to the axis so it hits the wall at an angle greater than c every time, so it is totally reflected and travels along the fibre with little loss.

practice: State what the critical angle is.
Calculate the critical angle for n = 1.33 (water).
Explain why total internal reflection cannot happen when light goes from air into glass.
independent: Core: Use readings from the semicircular block experiment to find c.
Extend: Calculate c for glass (n = 1.52) and for diamond (n = 2.42).
Stretch: Explain why diamond sparkles more than glass using critical angles.
exit: Define the critical angle.
Calculate c for n = 1.60.
Big question: when does light stop leaving the glass?
lessons.homework: Sketch an optical fibre and explain why the light stays in it using the idea of the critical angle.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a labelled three-ray diagram. Stretch: explain why fibres are surrounded by a cladding of lower refractive index (verify).

lessons.unit: Physics 4: Energy resources and energy transfers
lessons.title: Units of energy and power, convection in everyday life, and surfaces that radiate
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a sea breeze blow in the afternoon, and why do mosque domes and homes in hot countries often have light-coloured, shiny roofs?
objectives: State the units kg, J, m, m/s, m/s2, N, s and W
Explain everyday phenomena using convection
Relate emission and absorption of radiation to surface and temperature
successCriteria: All: give the unit of each energy quantity and name three convection examples
Most: explain a convection current using density
Some: compare surfaces and temperatures for emitting and absorbing radiation
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: sea breezes; Design technology: insulation
lessons.smsc: Moral: sensible use of energy and avoiding waste (israf)

keywords.def: transfer of thermal energy by the movement of heated fluid
object that gives out radiation
object that takes in radiation
unit of energy; one watt is one joule per second

starter: Bismillah. Name the three methods of thermal energy transfer.
State the equation for kinetic energy.
Calculate the power if 600 J is transferred in 20 s.

teach.heading: Units for energy and power
bullets: Energy and work: joule (J)
Power: watt (W) = J/s
Mass: kg; velocity: m/s; acceleration: m/s2
Force: N; distance: m; time: s
teach.note: Include a quick calculation to link the units: a 2.0 kg trolley at 3.0 m/s has KE = 0.5 x 2.0 x 3.0 squared = 9.0 J. Work done = force x distance, so N x m = J. Power = energy / time, so J/s = W. Ask pupils to track units through each step.

teach.heading: Convection in everyday life
bullets: Warm fluid expands and becomes less dense
It rises; cooler, denser fluid sinks
A convection current is set up
Examples: sea breeze, radiators, kettles, boilers
teach.note: Only in fluids (liquids and gases), not solids. Sea breeze: the land heats faster than the sea in the day, warm air rises over land, cooler air from the sea moves in. At night the pattern reverses. Immersion heaters are placed near the bottom of a tank so the warm water rises. Freezer compartments are at the top of a fridge so cold air sinks. Hot-air balloons rise because heated air is less dense.
cycle: It becomes less dense and rises
Cooler, denser fluid sinks to replace it

teach.heading: Worked example: explain a sea breeze
bullets: Link land heating to density
Name the movement of air
Complete the circuit of air
teach.note: Pupils lose marks for saying 'heat rises'; the accurate statement is that warm air is less dense and rises.

model.problem: Explain why a sea breeze blows from the sea to the land on a hot afternoon.
steps: The land heats up faster than the sea
Air above the land is heated, expands and becomes less dense
Cooler, denser air from the sea flows in to replace it
model.answer: A convection current: cool air moves from sea to land.

teach.heading: Check: radiators
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Option A is the trap 'heat rises' with no reasoning. Option C confuses conduction with convection.

check.q: Why is a room heated by a radiator warmed throughout?
options: the radiator conducts heat through the air
warm air rises and sets up a convection current
cold air rises and moves away
check.why: Air next to the radiator warms, becomes less dense and rises. Cooler air moves in, setting up a convection current.

teach.heading: Emitting and absorbing radiation
bullets: All objects emit infrared radiation
Hotter objects emit more radiation
Dark, matt surfaces: good emitters and absorbers
Light, shiny surfaces: poor emitters and absorbers
teach.note: Leslie cube: four faces (matt black, shiny black, matt white, shiny silver) at the same temperature; an infrared detector shows the matt black face emits most. Solar panels and radiator surfaces are dark and matt; emergency blankets and fire-fighter suits are shiny so they reflect radiation; houses in hot places are often painted white. Ask: why are the back of a fridge's pipes black and matt?

teach.heading: Temperature matters too
bullets: Higher temperature: more radiation per second
The surface of the Sun emits a lot
An object at room temperature emits infrared
Equal absorbing and emitting means constant temperature
teach.note: Link to the Earth: when the rate of absorbing equals the rate of emitting, the temperature stays constant; if absorption rises, the temperature goes up. Keep the idea qualitative.
